works.abstract: Combining multiple plant protein isolates (PPIs) in plant-based milk alternatives (PBMAs) may be able to increase protein concentration while avoiding specific negative sensory properties from single PPIs. This study employed a two-stage approach using soy, pea, and lupin protein isolates (4% w / v total). First, a simplex centroid mixture design combined with descriptive sensory analysis ( n = 8) was used to evaluate the sensory characteristics of protein blends, which identified four formulations with relatively neutral sensory profiles through multivariate analysis. Selected formulations were then subjected to industrial UHT processing and compared with non-UHT counterparts using descriptive sensory analysis, volatile profiling (GC–MS), and particle size measurements. UHT samples exhibited smaller particle size (D 4,3 = 1.54–1.74 μm) and were perceived more homogenous with reduced beany/floury attributes. Descriptive sensory analysis identified soy-pea or soy-dominant ternary blends for developing protein-enriched PBMAs with relatively neutral sensory profiles and reduced perception of undesirable attributes.

works.abstract: Sweet proteins represent a healthy alternative to refined sugar and non-nutritive sweeteners, but their thermostability limits several industrial food applications. We rationally designed 20 variants of Q-brazzein and thaumatin-II to enhance thermostability, expressing and testing 16 in vitro. Variants of both sweet proteins were identified with increased thermostability. Across all designed sweet protein variants, we found a significant inverse correlation between predicted ΔΔG and experimental Tm and a positive correlation between Tm and charge density. For thaumatin-II we identified a variant, Thau69, with 10 °C higher melting temperature. For Q-Brazzein we identified a variant, Braz110, that exhibited a melting point above 110 °C. Structural modelling of Braz110 indicated no interference with key amino acids important for sweetness or the interaction with the T1R2/T1R3 sweet taste receptor, which is supported by human consumer sensory evaluations. This study highlights the potential to design sweet protein variants with improved functionality for food applications.

Biopesticide-associated Bacillus thuringiensis on retail fresh produce: occurrence, typing and implications for food-safety surveillance
works.abstract: Bacillus thuringiensis is one of the most widely used microbial biopesticides and is likely to gain further relevance in the transformation of agrifood systems. However, as a member of B. cereus sensu lato ( B. cereus s.l. ), B. thuringiensis may harbor enterotoxin genes associated with diarrheal illness, raising food-safety concerns about its presence on minimally processed fresh produce. This study aimed to generate a surveillance-oriented retail dataset on the prevalence and genetic diversity of B. thuringiensis on retail fresh produce. A total of 280 fresh produce samples, including leafy greens, vegetables, and fruits, were collected from a retail distribution center in Switzerland, and presumptive B. cereus s.l. was enumerated according to ISO 7932:2004 (limit of detection, 5 CFU/g). Presumptive B. cereus s.l. isolates were subjected to PCR-based profiling of enterotoxin genes, and B. thuringiensis -associated insecticidal toxin genes ( cry genes). Selected isolates were further characterized by Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy for clustering, and a subset was analyzed by whole-genome sequencing for high-resolution comparison with commercially used biopesticide strains. B. thuringiensis was detected in 22% of produce samples and occurred at comparable frequencies across produce categories. Isolates predominantly showed biopesticide-associated profiles, and 20 out of 22 sequenced B. thuringiensis isolates showed close genomic relatedness to commercially used biopesticide strains. These findings provide a surveillance-relevant retail baseline for biopesticide-associated B. thuringiensis on fresh produce. The observed profiles are consistent with residues from B. thuringiensis -based biopesticides contributing to its occurrence at retail. Together, the results support improved interpretation of B. cereus s.l. findings in fresh-produce monitoring.

works.title: Multi-omics reveals the biosynthesis and pharmacological targets of antioxidant polyphenols in Polygonatum cyrtonema
works.abstract: Polygonatum cyrtonema Hua is a crucial medicinal and edible plant whose antioxidant activity is primarily attributed to its phenolic constituents. Evaluating samples from five geographical origins revealed that the Fuzhou (FZ) ecotype exhibited the strongest antioxidant capacity, significantly correlating with total phenolic content (TPC). Integrated metabolomics and co-expression network analyses identified 32 key polyphenols (flavonoids, lignans, and phenolic acids) as central contributors to this antioxidant capacity. Furthermore, network pharmacology and molecular docking predicted that 10 key polyphenols stably interact with core oxidative damage-related proteins, including prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2 (PTGS2), matrix metallopeptidase 9 (MMP9), and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). Transcriptomic profiling highlighted the enrichment of phenylpropanoid and flavonoid biosynthesis pathways across origins. Integrative analysis identified 14 structural genes driving polyphenol biosynthesis, with RT-qPCR confirming the upregulation of 4-coumarate : CoA ligase ( 4CL ), Chalcone synthase ( CHS ), Shikimic acid/Quinic acid hydroxycinnamoyl transferase ( HCT ), and Dirigent protein ( DIR ) in the FZ samples. Ultimately, this study elucidates the gene-metabolite basis of geographical variations in P. cyrtonema antioxidant capacity, providing valuable pharmacological insights and genetic resources for breeding superior, high-polyphenol cultivars.

Functional nanocomposites for Ochratoxin A removal from wine: design strategies, mechanisms, and application challenges
works.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
works.abstract: Ochratoxin A (OTA) contamination remains a major challenge for wine safety due to its high stability and toxicity. Conventional removal methods often compromise wine quality or face scalability limitations, whereas functional nanocomposites have emerged as an increasingly investigated approach for OTA removal. By integrating high-surface-area matrices, specific recognition elements, and stimuli-responsive components, these materials may address several limitations of traditional adsorbents. This review summarizes recent advances in functional nanocomposites for OTA removal from wine, highlighting key design strategies and representative material systems, including inorganic hybrids, crystalline porous frameworks, and multifunctional platforms. The underlying mechanisms and critical factors influencing adsorption performance in complex wine matrices are discussed, together with practical challenges related to material stability, sensory quality preservation, and biosafety. Although promising results have been achieved at the laboratory scale, commercialization is still limited by cost, performance stability, and regulatory uncertainties. Future research should emphasize green synthesis, rational material design, and comprehensive safety evaluation.

works.title: The future of storage stability for dried egg products: a synergistic control strategy based on green technologies
works.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
works.abstract: Dried egg products have broad application prospects due to their safety and portability. During processing, storage, and transportation, issues such as darkening color, loss of flavor, and reduced nutritional content can occur. These problems are mainly caused by lipid and protein oxidation, which influenced by processing technology, storage conditions, and water activity. This paper summarizes quality control strategies, including optimized microbial control achieved through irradiation and radio frequency-assisted thermal processing. Improving the storage stability of dried egg products using subcritical fluid extraction and supercritical carbon dioxide extraction for defatting, combined with modification methods (Maillard reaction modification and microencapsulation). The study explores drying methods to reduce oxidative deterioration and functional decline.Future research should focus on integrating mild processing, natural antioxidants, intelligent packaging, and synergistic non-thermal sterilization technologies. This review based on fundamental research on dried egg products, aims to synergistically enhance the quality, safety, and economic value of dried egg products, while also providing insights for other powdered foods.

works.title: Transitioning to a flexitarian diet: A mixed methods study exploring barriers, enablers and strategies to increasing family non-animal protein consumption among parents with children aged 6 months to 16 years in the UK
works.abstract: Shifting family dietary patterns to reduce meat and increase non-animal protein consumption is key to improving sustainability and health. We conducted a mixed-methods study exploring enablers, barriers and strategies to increasing family-level consumption of non-animal proteins and explored parental perceptions across a range of non-animal proteins. We integrated findings from qualitative focus groups (N = 32) and a large online questionnaire (N = 1013) with parents of children aged 6 months-16 years in the UK. Cost, lack of convenience and perceived high levels of processing were identified as important barriers for parents. However, incorporating non-animal proteins into familiar family meals to increase dietary variety and improve affordability enabled greater consumption. Our integrated findings suggest that strategies to increase non-animal protein consumption among UK families are likely to be more acceptable if they align with existing family routines and support incremental dietary change through suitable substitutions and hybrid approaches that combine animal and non-animal ingredients.

works.abstract: Postharvest fruit deterioration is mainly driven by ethylene accumulation, oxidative damage, water loss and microbial infection. Here, we developed a biodegradable composite film made from sodium carboxymethyl cellulose and tannic acid, named CMC@TA, for active fruit preservation. Boltz-2 predicted TA binding near the Fe 2+ -associated catalytic region of ACC oxidase. Isothermal titration calorimetry indicated TA-ACO binding (Kd = 9.93 μM), while cellular imaging showed overlapping signals. The CMC@TA film showed antioxidant, water-retention and broad-spectrum antimicrobial activities. Compared with polyethylene (PE) wrapping, CMC@TA reduced ethylene emission by 14% in bananas and 71% in hardy kiwifruits after six days. Relative to PE, CMC@TA reduced weight loss by 36–46% in climacteric and 40–45% in non-climacteric fruits, and prolonged climacteric fruit shelf life by 25–60%. Preservation improved in seven fruit species. Soil degradation, sprout growth and drinking-water exposure assays confirmed its biodegradability and biosafety. This work provides a mechanism-guided packaging strategy for reducing fruit loss.

works.abstract: Egg yolk plasma is the main contributor to the emulsifying and gelling properties of egg yolk. Despite its functional importance, and although extensive physicochemical studies have been conducted, further in-depth characterization of its colloidal components, namely the low-density lipoproteins (LDLs), is needed. In this study, egg yolk plasma was prepared at two ionic strengths (0.1 and 0.2 M NaCl) and centrifuged at 10,000 or 40,000 × g to investigate the influence of extraction conditions on composition, structure, and functionality. Increasing NaCl reduced plasma lipid content and increased the relative abundance of LDL apoproteins. Increasing centrifugal force increased the proportion of neutral lipids and decreased the proportion of polar lipids. Despite these compositional differences, dynamic light scattering and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) consistently showed a dominant LDL population centered at 40-50 nm across all conditions, indicating structural robustness. The SAXS data were successfully described using a core-shell model, supporting a low-electron-density lipid core surrounded by a protein- and phospholipid-rich shell, with dimensions consistent across treatments. Temperature-dependent SAXS showed that LDL particles remained structurally stable up to ∼65 °C, above which they showed increased interparticle aggregation, followed by pronounced anisotropy and restructuring above ∼70 °C. Plasma prepared at 40,000 × g formed the stiffest heat-induced gels, whereas plasma prepared at 10,000 × g reached lower equilibrium interfacial tension and higher interfacial viscoelastic moduli at equal protein concentration. Overall, moderate variations in extraction conditions did not alter LDL structure but induced compositional changes that modulated interparticle interactions and functionality, supporting the view of egg yolk plasma as a structurally robust yet functionally tunable colloidal system.

works.abstract: Reliable in vitro methods are needed to accurately assess protein digestibility. Sulfosalicylic acid (SSA) (4.5%) and methanol (80%) fractionation were applied to in vitro digesta (INFOGEST 2.0) of 15 N-labelled micellar casein and mashed faba bean meals (5.2 and 8.5% of protein content) to measure real in vitro protein digestibility (RIVPD) in comparison with human values. The peptide molecular size distribution of bioaccessible fractions and MWCO were determined by size exclusion chromatography and compared with that obtained after tangential filtration. The use of 15 N-labelled protein enabled the precise quantification of dietary and endogenous N in the non-bioaccessible fraction. RIVPD was compared with the human real ileal protein digestibility on the same dietary protein sources. For a given meal, chemical fractionations and tangential filtration had non-significantly different MWCOs (<6 kDa for casein and <3 kDa for faba bean). For both meals and chemical fractionations, the RIVPD was close to the human values (<3.3% points of difference) in a non-significant manner ( p > 0.05) except for casein at 5.2% (3% points of difference, p < 0.05). In the non-bioaccessible fraction, N was mainly of endogenous origin and depended on the dietary protein content (79 ± 9 vs. 70 ± 13% for 5.2 and 8.5% of protein content), but accounted only for 35 ± 5% (faba bean) down to 22 ± 6% (casein) of total endogenous N. This study suggests that in vitro digestion combined with chemical fractionation can give reliable estimate of protein digestibility as determined on two 15 N-labelled protein sources. This should however be further validated.

Bacterial and fungal community dynamics in black pepper (Piper nigrum) across different processing plants using culture-based and amplicon sequencing approaches
works.abstract: Black pepper (Piper nigrum) is among the most commercially relevant spices worldwide, yet its microbial ecology throughout processing remains insufficiently understood, particularly in relation to food safety. Despite being a low-water-activity product, black pepper may harbor diverse bacterial and fungal communities, including spoilage microorganisms, mycotoxigenic fungi, and foodborne pathogens. In this study, we investigated the dynamics of bacterial and fungal communities along the black pepper processing chain in three distinct processing plants. A total of 154 samples were collected from processing plants A, B, and C in São Mateus, Espírito Santo, Brazil. Culture-dependent analyses included enumeration of aerobic mesophilic bacteria, Enterobacteriaceae, lactic acid bacteria, total fungi, and xerophilic fungi; fungal isolation and identification; and Salmonella detection and confirmation. Culture-independent profiling was performed by amplicon sequencing targeting the V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene and the V9 region of the 18S rRNA gene. Microbial counts increased throughout processing, indicating that post-drying operations represent critical contamination points. Fungal isolation revealed genera of hygienic and toxicological relevance, including Aspergillus, Fusarium, Penicillium, and Cladosporium. Salmonella was detected in 14.3% of the samples, comprising nine serotypes, with the highest occurrence after drying. Amplicon sequencing identified 5 phyla and 85 genera in the fungal community, whereas for the bacterial community, 24 phyla and 475 genera were identified, with Ascomycota, Proteobacteria and Firmicutes predominating across samples. Alpha and beta diversity analyses demonstrated significant differences among processing plants and confirmed processing as a major driver of microbial community assembly. Collectively, these findings reveal processing-associated microbial shifts and underscore the urgent need for improved hygienic practices, targeted monitoring, and effective decontamination strategies for black pepper.

works.journal: Annual Review of Food Science and Technology
works.abstract: Food formulation requires balancing taste, nutrition, sustainability, and cost. Traditionally, new foods have emerged through empirical experimentation, expert intuition, and iterative refinement. Now, artificial intelligence (AI) offers the opportunity to accelerate this process. Yet despite rapid advances across food science, most AI applications remain isolated prediction and optimization tasks rather than parts of a broader scientific approach. Here we integrate these emerging technologies into a unified framework-the generative science of food formulation-in which digital food representations enable AI to predict, discover, generate, organize, simulate, and optimize. We illustrate this approach through sustainability and nutrition, where generative AI transforms environmental and nutritional metrics from post hoc evaluation criteria into explicit design objectives. Finally, we identify the data, models, benchmarks, and automation that will establish computational food design as a rigorous scientific discipline. Together, these advances have the potential to transform food formulation from an empirical discipline into a generative science.

The rise of electrospinning technology: moving forward to the development, production, and application of food packaging
works.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
works.abstract: Environmental pollution caused by conventional food packaging has become a growing concern, as most packaging materials are still plastic based. Current research is focused on developing sustainable alternatives and designing functional packaging systems. However, functional ingredients are usually thermally unstable, and the heating step commonly involved in film preparation can compromise their stability. Electrospinning has attracted increasing attention as a non-thermal processing technique for food packaging applications. This review compares and highlights the different sustainable material used in food packaging electrospun fibrous films including an overview of applications in food packaging and a review of electrospun films categorized by their functional performance. Overall, proteins, polysaccharides, and their complexes are promising sustainable candidates for electrospun fibrous film fabrication. With the incorporation of functional ingredients, electrospun fibrous films can be designed with added functionalities, including antibacterial and antioxidant activity as well as freshness indication. Moreover, their high specific surface area and porous structure can support prolonged food preservation. Nevertheless, further work is still required to enable large-scale production and to improve physical performance, which will be essential for advancing electrospun packaging toward practical use.

works.title: Small matters: the effect of particle size on food analysis, sensory perception, and nutrient release during digestion
works.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
works.abstract: Nutrients in foods are embedded within complex plant structures or structural microdomains that influence their chemical and nutritional behavior, a concept known as the food matrix effect (FME). The FME explains why foods with similar nutrient compositions can behave differently depending on how nutrients are confined and interact within their structural domains. The food matrix can act as a barrier, limiting access of solvents and enzymes to nutrients during digestion. Reducing particle size increases surface area exposure, alters matrix–nutrient interactions, and ultimately improves extraction efficiency and the quantitative measurement of specific food components. This not only improves analytical accuracy but also affects sensory perception and nutrient bioavailability during digestion. Finer particles seem to predominantly promote faster enzymatic breakdown, better nutrient absorption, and distinct textural and flavor attributes, depending on the food matrix and structural constraints. However, intensive grinding may induce physical and chemical changes that alter the original state of food components. Together, these effects lead to inconsistencies across studies that rely on particle-size reduction. Consequently, standardizing size-reduction protocols, accurately characterizing particle size, and determining possible physicochemical changes are imperative to ensure reproducible and meaningful results. This article highlights how particle size critically influences food analysis, sensory qualities, and nutritional evaluation, emphasizing that food research should systematically report size-reduction outcomes and consider their effects when interpreting both analytical and physiological results.

The intention-behaviour gap in pro-environmental food consumption: a cross-cultural analysis using an extended Theory of Planned Behaviour
works.abstract: Despite increasing environmental awareness among consumers, a significant gap persists between intention and actual purchasing behaviour in the context of pro-environmental foods. This study extends the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) by integrating perceived behavioural control, willingness to pay, and trust in certifications into the post-intention phase of the model. It examines their roles both as direct antecedents of behaviour and as potential moderators of the intention - behaviour relationship to explain why intention does not always translate into action. Using hierarchical structural equation modelling (SEM) and multigroup analysis on a sample of 2016 consumers from the United States and Spain, the results provide strong support for the proposed model. Perceived behavioural control and willingness to pay operate as direct antecedents of behaviour (acting as structural and economic prerequisites) rather than as moderators. In contrast, trust emerges as the only significant moderator facilitating the conversion of intention into purchase behaviour. Significant cultural differences are observed in the relative weight of these mechanisms, reflecting distinct sensitivities to price and intention formation across markets. These findings suggest that promoting pro-environmental food consumption requires more than strengthening positive intentions. Effective strategies must reduce situational barriers and be tailored to cultural contexts to translate latent intentions into sustainable behaviour.

works.title: Spatially resolved accumulation of metabolites in Chaenomeles speciosa revealed by MALDI-MSI and laser microdissection coupled with UPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS
works.abstract: Chaenomeles speciosa fruit has medicinal and edible value; however, the spatial distribution of its bioactive metabolites remains largely unexplored. In this study, we integrated chemical composition analysis, MALDI-MSI, and LMD-UPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS to systematically investigate the spatial distribution of metabolites across different tissue microregions of Ch. speciosa fruits. A total of 313 DAMs were detected using MALDI-MSI, and fuzzy c-means clustering categorized these DAMs into ten distinct spatial distribution patterns. Laser microdissection coupled with UPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS was further used to validate the spatial distribution results. Phenolics were predominantly enriched in the peripheral receptacle tissues and dorsal carpel bundles, whereas saccharides and amino acids were relatively uniformly distributed. Triterpenoids, such as ursolic and oleanolic acids, exhibited strong tissue specificity and mainly accumulated in the cuticle and peripheral tissues. This study provides a spatial metabolomic landscape of Ch. speciosa fruits at the microregional scale, thus establishing a foundation for quality evaluation and targeted utilization.

works.abstract: Sea buckthorn fruit quality varies with tree age, but the molecular relationships between branches and fruits remain unclear. This study characterized age-dependent changes in fruit quality and branch–fruit associations in 4-year-old, 5-year-old, and 6-year-old sea buckthorn ( Hippophae rhamnoides L.) using phenotypic analysis, targeted and untargeted metabolomics, transcriptomics, and weighted gene co-expression network analysis. Fruit weight increased from 0.38 g at 4 years to 0.54 g at 6 years ( p < 0.001), and 6-year-old fruits had the highest redness value (a* = 18.54). Vitamin C decreased from 0.46 to 0.41 g/100 g ( p < 0.001), whereas procyanidin B4 increased from 78.19 to 103.30 ng/100 mg ( p = 0.044). Untargeted metabolomics identified 554 and 238 DEMs in fruit and 1283 and 996 DEMs in branches for the 5-vs.-4-year and 6-vs.-5-year comparisons, respectively. Branch transcriptomics identified 2658 and 2464 DEGs. Integrated WGCNA and pathway analyses revealed distinct age-associated patterns involving PRKAA and PP2C during 4-5 years and MYBP and PIP5K during 5-6 years, which were associated with fruit metabolite changes. These findings indicate age-dependent coordination between branch molecular responses and fruit quality and provide a basis for optimizing sea buckthorn harvesting and utilization.

works.abstract: Brining of kimchi cabbage is a key process. However, the effect of brining conditions on the tissue-associated population and intra-tissue localization of pathogens remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how brining conditions affect the quality of kimchi cabbage, as well as the tissue-associated population and intra-tissue localization of Escherichia coli O157:H7 associated with the kimchi cabbage tissue. Cut kimchi cabbage was salted at 4–16% salt concentrations for 1–4 h at 4–20 °C, followed by one to three washes. Physicochemical properties were analyzed, E. coli O157:H7 was quantified using culture-based methods, and its distribution was examined via immunohistochemical analysis. Salt concentration and brining time significantly influenced total soluble solids, salinity, moisture content, pH, and titratable acidity (all p < 0.05). Temperature did not significantly affect these parameters ( p > 0.05), and number of washing steps only significantly affected the pH ( p < 0.05). Increasing the salt concentration from 4% to 16% resulted in an estimated reduction of 0.77 log CFU/g in the E. coli O157:H7 population associated with the kimchi cabbage tissue; brining time, temperature, and number of washing steps did not significantly affect the tissue-associated population. In the immunohistochemical analysis, DAB-positive signals were distributed unevenly, appearing more frequently on cut surfaces and within vascular tissues than on intact epidermal surfaces. In longitudinal sections, the frequency of signals decreased with distance from the cut surface. These findings indicate that, despite significant physicochemical changes induced at higher salt concentrations, the reduction in the tissue-associated E. coli population remained limited.

Relationship between dietary inflammatory potential, cardiometabolic risk factors, and inflammatory markers among Brazilian adults: a cross-sectional study
works.abstract: Diet plays an essential role in modulating systemic inflammation. Exposure to a pro-inflammatory diet heightens inflammatory responses and, consequently, increases the risk of developing various noncommunicable chronic diseases (NCDs). Despite the high prevalence of pro-inflammatory dietary patterns and cardiometabolic risk factors among Brazilian adults, few studies have simultaneously evaluated their association with inflammatory markers in this population. This is a cross-sectional study conducted at a public university ( n = 558), including both sexes, aged 20–60 years. Sociodemographic, anthropometric, and clinical characteristics were collected, including interleukins, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), C-reactive protein (CRP), lipid and glycemic profile, body mass index (BMI), and waist circumference (WC). The dietary intake data were obtained from two 24 h dietary recalls, whose data (grams/ml) were entered into the Nutrition Data System for Research (NDS-R) software by trained researchers. Dietary inflammatory potential was assessed using the Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII), divided into tertiles. DII scores ranged from −3.41 to +5.38 (mean ± SD: 1.15 ± 1.73), indicating a predominantly pro-inflammatory diet. Regression analyses showed that higher DII scores were statistically significantly associated with higher BMI (>T1- ≤ T2: β = 1.14, 95%CI:0.07–2.22; >T2: β = 2.37, 95%CI:1.27–3.46), diastolic blood pressure (DBP; >T2: β = 2.79, 95%CI:0.93–4.65), CRP levels (>T2: β = 1.50, 95%CI:0.54–2.46), WC (>T2:PR = 1.47, 95%CI:1.14–1.89), waist-to-hip ratio (WHR; >T1- ≤ T2:PR = 1.24, 95%CI:1.05–1.48; >T2:PR = 1.23, 95%CI:1.03–1.48), and Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance (HOMA-IR; >T1- ≤ T2:PR = 1.35, 95%CI:1.03–1.79; >T2:PR = 1.67, 95%CI:1.27–2.20). Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to assess the impact of dietary shifts toward anti-inflammatory patterns on reducing systemic inflammation and cardiometabolic risk in the Brazilian population, thereby guiding targeted nutritional strategies aimed at mitigating diet-related inflammation and preventing NCDs.

Lactose as disaccharide drives gut microbiota remodelling and metabolic adaptations in young mice
works.abstract: Extended breastfeeding has health benefits for the offspring's later life, but whether this is due to the disaccharide lactose or its monosaccharide constituents remains elusive. This study integrated physiological parameters, intestinal morphology and transcriptomic profiles, and gut microbiota compositions of weaned mice fed isocaloric diets containing (32 energy %) glucose (Glu group), glucose + galactose (Gal, representing hydrolysed lactose) or lactose (Lac) for three weeks. Lac mice showed lower body weight, mainly due to lower food intake and body weight gain in the first week. This was accompanied by small intestine (SI) elongation and caecal enlargement in Lac mice, suggesting adapted nutrient absorption and fermentation capacity. At whole-body level, Lac mice showed lower 24 h energy expenditure (EE) and lower glucose oxidation, while Gal mice showed higher lipid oxidation versus Lac and Glu, with similar EE versus Glu. SI RNA sequencing revealed in Lac mice higher transcript abundances in SI fatty acid oxidation pathways, which diverged from the transcriptomic effects in Gal. Furthermore, Lac but not Gal mice markedly shifted gut microbiota composition versus Glu mice: lower bacterial diversity with higher abundance of genera associated with beneficial metabolic effects, e.g. Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium , and lower potential pro-inflammatory Ruminococcus . Conclusively, extended lactose intake triggers a series of intestinal morphological, physiological and transcriptomic adaptations together with gut microbial changes, which are different from the effects seen by its monosaccharide constituents. This emphasises the unique role of lactose in post-weaning development and metabolism, highlighting and extending lactose's role beyond its energy content and constituents.

Seasonal dynamics in lettuce phyllosphere microbiota and potential transfer to the human gut
works.abstract: Abstract The surface of fresh vegetable leaves harbors diverse microorganisms with the potential to influence human health through the microbiome-food-gut axis. We investigated the ecology of the bacterial and fungal microbiota on green and red lettuces (n = 143) for a 12-month period using high-throughput amplicon sequencing, and assessed the potential transfer of these microbiota to the human gut. Lettuce-associated fungal and bacterial microbiota exhibited substantial temporal variation, converging into two distinct seasonal cycles: early-season (S1) and late-season (S2). Seasonal progression from S1 to S2 increased species richness in season-specific fungal and bacterial taxa, while inducing abundance shifts in persistent fungal taxa and compositional shifts in persistent bacterial taxa. These seasonal dynamics resulted in more complex and stable microbial networks, in which potential pathogen-associated fungal genera were less frequently enriched. Comparative analyses with gut microbiota datasets from 2831 (fungal) and 3254 (bacterial) individuals revealed that lettuce-associated fungal and bacterial taxa were widely detected in the human gut, with bacterial taxa detected more frequently than fungal taxa. Season-specific taxa were detected more frequently than persistent taxa, and microbial assembly in the gut was shaped by both neutral and deterministic processes. Notably, lettuce-associated bacterial taxa predominantly co-occurred with non-plant glycan-degrading commensal bacteria in a season-dependent manner, and enrichment of these co-occurring taxa correlated positively with gut microbiota richness and composition. Our findings provide insights into the ecological linkages between fresh vegetable microbiota and the human gut microbiota through the food-gut axis.

works.abstract: Modulating the gut microbiome through diet could positively influence mental health, offering new perspectives for dietary approaches in the treatment and prevention of mental disorders. Many lactic acid bacteria (LAB) found in fermented food are major microbial producers of neuroactive compounds. Three LAB strains, Limosilactobacillus (Lmb.) fermentum TO24, Levilactobacillus (Lvb.) brevis TO10, and Lentilactobacillus (Llb.) diolivorans B92, previously isolated from fermented foods, were used to ferment a plant-based matrix to develop a plant-based yogurt-like (pYL) product. We demonstrated that the strains were able to produce neuroactive compounds during fermentation and that remained stable during refrigerated storage of the pYL. The pYL was administered daily for 11 days to a m-SHIME® model simulating the gut microbiome of a depressed patient. The abundance of the pYL strains Lvb. brevis and Lmb. fermentum increased during treatment in both the lumen and mucosa samples, with Lvb. brevis persisting after the washout phase. The pYL treatment significantly inhibited potentially pro-inflammatory taxa ( Acidaminococcus intestini and Megasphaera massiliensis ) in both compartments. Notably, the neuroactive potential was not limited to the introduced strains. A significant functional redundancy emerged, as commensal Metagenome-Assembled Genomes (MAGs) were associated with key functional hubs involved in GABA biosynthesis. These encouraging findings suggest that the pYL treatment can modulate and partially restore the dysbiotic gut microbiome in depressed patients. Gut microbiome modulation through fermented foods consumption may represent a viable therapeutic strategy for mitigating mental diseases.

Effect of lipase pretreatment on protein hydrolysis of dry-cured ham skin for the production of bioactive hydrolysates
works.abstract: Dry-cured ham processing generates large amounts of skin by-products, which have great potential as sources of value-added ingredients due to its high collagen content. However, the high fat and salt contents of this matrix can limit hydrolysis efficiency, highlighting the need for effective pretreatment strategies. In this study, a novel Lecitase Ultra (LU) pretreatment was combined with Alcalase or Collagenase hydrolysis as a sustainable approach to improve the generation of bioactive hydrolysates. Sequential water-ethanol reduced fat content from 53% to 17% and achieved 75% Na + removal, providing an effective defatting and desalting strategy of dry-cured ham skin prior to enzymatic treatments. The LU pretreatment and type of protease used significantly influenced the free fatty acids (FFAs) and peptide profiles, thereby influencing the bioactivity of the hydrolysates. Collagenase showed the highest degree of hydrolysis (16%), whereas Alcalase hydrolysates, with and without LU pretreatment, generally presented the highest antioxidant activity and approximately 90% inhibition of Insulin-degrading enzyme. Collagenase hydrolysate without LU pretreatment showed the highest Dipeptidyl Peptidase-IV inhibition (64%), whereas pancreatic lipase inhibition (12%) was detected only after LU pretreatment. The obtained results demonstrate that sequential water–ethanol treatment combined with enzymatic hydrolysis represents a promising strategy for the sustainable valorisation of dry-cured ham skin. The differential effects of LU and proteases on peptide and FFA profiles and bioactivity highlight the potential for obtaining hydrolysates with specific functional properties, supporting applications as ingredients in food, feed, or cosmetic formulations.

Plasma-Based Technologies for Aquatic Product Preservation: Balancing Microbial Control and Oxidative Deterioration
works.abstract: : Background Aquatic products are highly nutritious but are particularly susceptible to microbial contamination, lipid oxidation, and protein degradation during postharvest handling and storage, posing challenges to food safety, quality preservation, and sustainable cold-chain logistics. Atmospheric cold plasma (ACP) and plasma-activated liquids (PALs), particularly plasma-activated water (PAW), have emerged as promising non-thermal preservation technologies because they generate reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS) capable of inactivating microorganisms while minimizing thermal damage. Scope and approach This review critically summarizes recent advances in the application of ACP and PALs for aquatic product preservation, with particular emphasis on the mechanisms underlying microbial inactivation and the complex interactions among microorganisms, proteins, lipids, and plasma-generated reactive species. Rather than considering microbial safety and quality independently, this review highlights how ACP simultaneously regulates microbial growth, protein oxidation, lipid oxidation, and volatile flavor formation, thereby determining the overall preservation outcome. Key findings and conclusions Current evidence indicates that the efficacy of ACP is highly dependent on treatment intensity, plasma operating conditions, and food matrix characteristics, requiring a careful balance between effective microbial control and the prevention of excessive oxidative deterioration. The review further discusses key barriers to industrial implementation, including the lack of standardized processing protocols, insufficient dose–response characterization, limited toxicological evidence, equipment scalability, and regulatory uncertainty. Finally, future research priorities are proposed, including mechanism-driven process optimization, standardized plasma characterization, multi-omics-assisted mechanistic studies, and the integration of ACP with plasma-activated liquids and other multi-hurdle preservation strategies. By critically synthesizing current evidence and identifying knowledge gaps that hinder industrial translation, this review provides a framework for developing standardized, sustainable, and intelligent plasma-based preservation systems for aquatic products.

Persistent Biofilms in the Food Industry: Mechanistic Insights, Emerging Interventions, and Smart Processing Frontiers.
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Biofilms are a major microbiological concern in the food and beverage industry because microorganisms can attach to food-contact surfaces, processing equipment, and other industrial environments despite routine cleaning and sanitation. Once established, biofilms develop an extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix that provides structural stability and protection against mechanical removal, antimicrobial agents, and adverse environmental conditions. Their persistence can facilitate the survival and dissemination of microbial cells and spores, increasing the risk of cross-contamination, foodborne illness, spoilage, reduced shelf life, product recalls, and economic losses. Scope and approach This review provides a comprehensive overview of biofilms in food and beverage processing environments, focusing on mechanisms underlying biofilm formation and persistence, their implications for food safety and product quality, and their industrial significance. It focuses on major pathogenic and spoilage-associated microorganisms that form biofilms, such as Listeria monocytogenes , Salmonella , Escherichia coli , Pseudomonas , Staphylococcus aureus , Bacillus , Geobacillus , and Alicyclobacillus . The review further examines current approaches for biofilm detection and characterization and evaluates emerging anti-biofilm technologies, including ozone, cold plasma, bacteriophages, biosurfactants, nanotechnology, and multi-hurdle strategies. Key findings and conclusions Conventional sanitation may be inadequate against mature biofilms, highlighting the need for integrated monitoring and control. Emerging technologies show potential as alternative or complementary interventions. Key challenges remain in standardizing detection methods, understanding multispecies and spore-associated biofilms, validating technologies under industrial conditions, and developing appropriate regulatory frameworks. Future research should focus on multispecies and spore-associated biofilms, industrial validation, advanced diagnostics, and multi-hurdle strategies to enable possible biofilm prevention and control in food-processing systems.

From production to post-ingestion transformation: Tracing compositional changes in rice bran protein hydrolysates
Ultrasound as a Multifunctional Physical Platform for Whole‐Grape Valorization: From Field Management to Green Extraction, Quality Modulation, and Intelligent Scale‐Up
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: The grape and wine industry faces prolonged barrel aging, microbial spoilage, protein haze, chemical additives, and inefficient by-product valorization. These challenges motivate nonthermal technologies that reduce chemical inputs. Ultrasound operates in two mechanistically distinct regimes: sensing, based on acoustic propagation, reflection, and echo detection, and processing, driven mainly by acoustic cavitation and its physical and chemical effects, including microjets, shock waves, localized hotspots, and reactive radicals. These complementary modes provide a versatile physical platform. This review covers ultrasound across the grape-wine continuum: acoustic imaging for precision viticulture; postharvest preservation with green activated water; green extraction enhanced by natural deep eutectic solvents; grape protein modification for ingredient assembly; modulation of wine color, aroma, and colloidal stability; selected aging-associated reactions involving 1-hydroxyethyl radicals; selective microbial inactivation and fermentation modulation; and scale-up based on energy characterization, continuous-flow reactors, and data-driven modeling. Current evidence indicates that ultrasound is evolving from an empirically optimized unit operation toward a mechanistically informed and quantitatively characterized physical-field platform. Reported effects include accelerated aging-related transformations, modified protein structure and stability, and selective microbial responses, although they depend on treatment conditions and matrix properties. Absorbed energy density supports quantitative comparison of treatments, but reliable scale-up also requires acoustic-field distribution, residence time, temperature, and reactor geometry. Future progress will require standardized energy reporting, pilot- and continuous-flow validation, physics-informed data-driven modeling, and integration of process analytical technologies with closed-loop control. These advances would support more reproducible, scalable, and sustainable ultrasound processing in the grape and wine sector.

works.title: Vitamin B12 Biofortification of Plant‐Based Foods Through Fermentation With Propionibacterium freudenreichii : Mechanisms, Challenges, and Opportunities
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Vitamin B12 (VB12) is essential for human health but occurs predominantly in animal-derived foods, posing a challenge for adequate intake on plant-based diets. Fermentation with Propionibacterium freudenreichii offers a route to in situ fortification, in which the vitamin is generated within the food matrix rather than added as a purified fortificant, eliminating the separation and purification steps required for industrial production. This review examines the mechanistic and technological basis of that approach. It sets out the chemical and physiological requirements any dietary VB12 source must satisfy, and the analytical consequence that follows: microbiological assays cannot distinguish bioactive cobalamin from inactive analogs, so reported concentrations in fermented plant foods require confirmation by chromatographic or mass-spectrometric methods. It then summarizes VB12 biosynthesis in P. freudenreichii, the factors governing its production, and applications across cereals, legumes, side-streams and other plant matrices. Substrate composition, particularly cobalt availability and pH-buffering capacity, together with oxygen supply and the choice of cofermenting strains, largely determines yield. Recent fungal-bacterial cofermentations have reached concentrations exceeding earlier plant-based fermentations by more than an order of magnitude, indicating that nutritionally sufficient concentrations are attainable. Digestive release rather than synthesis now appears the more consequential constraint: in vitro bioaccessibility is high in processed products but substantially lower in unprocessed fermented material, pointing to cell disruption during processing as the determining step. Scale-up beyond pilot demonstrations and economic competitiveness remain unresolved, and no controlled human trial has yet evaluated the bioavailability of in situ synthesized VB12-the decisive step before any nutritional claim can be made.

works.title: From Printability to Product Quality in 3D and 4D Food Printing: Evidence, Comparability, and Translation
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) and four-dimensional (4D) food printing technologies have evolved from shape-making demonstrations to digitally controlled food production. However, comparative literature remains challenging due to incomplete reporting on material preparation, rheological experimental protocols, printer configurations, and product quality measurements. Furthermore, food-related findings are often discussed alongside non-food engineering concepts, lacking a clear distinction in the weight of evidence. This review analyzes the entire production chain, from material preparation and rheological characterization to printer operation, printed product quality, and application deployment. At each stage, we examine whether reported results are supported by adequate testing conditions, controls, variability estimates, and food-related evidence. Reported rheological ranges cannot define a universal printability window, as their meaning depends on measurement and printing conditions. A printed food can only be classified as 4D food if its response is intentionally programmed during printing, activated by specific stimuli, measured over time, and repeated across different samples. Evidence regarding sensory acceptability, clinical application, hygiene, shelf life, yield, and resource utilization is far less mature than evidence regarding geometric feasibility. In summary, existing literature supports conditional material-process relationships rather than validated universal models. Integrating the information needed to interpret and reproduce these relationships by domain of evidence allows for the differentiation of findings from food validation studies from specific system observations and engineering assumptions that still require testing in edible systems.

works.title: Dietary Organosulfur‐Containing Compounds (DOSCs) as Healthy Longevity Agents: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Future Perspectives
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Aging is a complex biological process characterized by a gradual decline in physiological functions and increased risk of chronic diseases. The framework of "hallmarks of aging" provides a foundation for identifying actionable targets to delay aging and extend healthspan. Among dietary interventions, bioactive compounds may modulate aging-related pathways. Dietary organosulfur-containing compounds (DOSCs), abundant in Allium vegetables, Brassicaceae species and moringa, and other natural sources (e.g., stink and djenkol beans, shiitake mushrooms), have attracted significant attention due to their pleiotropic health-promoting properties. Historically used in traditional medicine, DOSCs are now recognized for their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, cardioprotective, and neuroprotective activities. Our review conducts a comprehensive analysis of current knowledge on DOSCs as potential antiaging agents. We first outline their classification, dietary sources, and derivatives formed during food processing (particularly heat treatment and fermentation), highlighting how culinary practices modulate their concentrations and biological efficacy. Additionally, preclinical studies in model organisms and clinical investigations demonstrate that DOSCs can attenuate oxidative damage, improve mitochondrial function, modulate inflammatory signaling, and enhance resilience against age-related decline. Mechanistic insights suggest that DOSCs influence multiple hallmarks of aging. Despite promising findings, challenges remain regarding their bioavailability, interindividual variability, and limited long-term human data. Therefore, innovative strategies such as novel delivery systems, personalized nutrition, combination therapies with established geroprotective agents, and AI-driven compound discovery may accelerate the translational potential of DOSCs. Collectively, our review underscores DOSCs as a versatile and underexplored class of secondary dietary bioactive compounds with significant potential in extending lifespan and mitigating age-related disorders.

works.title: Nano‐Enabled Postbiotics in Functional Foods: Stability Challenges, Gastrointestinal Fate, and Translational Perspectives
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: The increasing demand for preventive and personalized nutrition has driven rapid growth in functional food development. These foods are designed not only to provide basic nutrition but also to deliver health-promoting bioactive compounds at specific sites. Postbiotics comprise nonviable microbial cells, cell components, and microbial metabolites. They have emerged as promising alternatives to live probiotics because of their improved safety, stability, and well-defined biological functions. These components can support epithelial barrier integrity, metabolic regulation, and immune modulation. However, their application in functional foods remains limited by poor stability, gastrointestinal (GI) degradation, food-matrix interactions, and low bioavailability following oral administration. This review discusses the major physicochemical and biological barriers affecting postbiotic stability and functionality. These include thermal degradation, pH instability, enzymatic breakdown, food-matrix interactions, and storage-related losses. It also highlights nano-enabled delivery systems for improving postbiotic delivery. The main systems include liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, nanogels, nanoemulsions, and solid lipid nanoparticles. Among these, nanoemulsions may offer comparatively greater translational promise for food applications because of their established processing, scalability, and compatibility with liquid and semisolid food matrices. Although the suitability of nanoemulsions depends on postbiotic properties and remains constrained by interfacial instability, oxidation, and food-matrix interactions. These systems can improve protection, controlled release, GI targeting, and epithelial uptake. However, regulatory uncertainty, scale-up challenges, economic constraints, and limited clinical evidence continue to hinder practical application. Future progress will depend on standardized characterization methods, long-term clinical validation, comprehensive safety assessment, scalable manufacturing, regulatory harmonization, and commercialization.

works.title: Density Functional Theory for Food Sensing: Mechanisms, Materials, and Multi‐Scale Integrations
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: With the rapid development of food sensing technologies, it has become increasingly important to understand the microscopic interactions that govern sensing performance. Traditional characterization methods often struggle to resolve critical mechanisms at the molecular level including adsorption behaviors, charge-transfer pathways, and electronic-structure changes. Consequently, density functional theory (DFT) has gained prominence for providing quantum-level insights into material-analyte interactions in food sensing. While recent reviews address individual sensing modalities or material design, none provides a unified framework for food-relevant sensing types. This review analyzes DFT from both theoretical and mechanistic perspectives in food sensing. It outlines the important results obtained from DFT calculations and explores its key role in revealing sensing mechanisms of different sensing types and materials, which establishes a framework connecting quantum-level analysis with sensing performance in food systems. Furthermore, emerging hybrid strategies coupling DFT with molecular docking, molecular dynamics, and deep learning models to expand capabilities are expected to enhance predictive capability and accelerate the development of intelligent, high-performance food sensing technologies.

works.title: Microbial Safety of Pecans: Contamination Pathways, Postharvest Interventions, and Food Safety Applications of Pecan Shells
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Pecans are a valuable commodity in North America but have been implicated in multiple recalls, primarily linked to Salmonella contamination. Pathogenic contamination can occur at multiple points along the production chain from farm to postharvest processing. Pecans remain a food safety concern because of their association with Salmonella-related recalls and the pathogen's ability to infiltrate in-shell pecans during postharvest handling and survive for extended periods. Therefore, various thermal and nonthermal postharvest treatments exist for their decontamination. This review summarizes the routes of microbial contamination in pecans, traditional and emerging strategies employed to inactivate pathogens, as well as the potential use of pecan shell by-products for food safety. Thermal treatments, such as hot water, steam, hot air, and oil roasting, have demonstrated effective inactivation of foodborne pathogens on in-shell pecans and kernels under specific treatment conditions with minimal changes to the nuts' quality parameters. Chemical sanitizers generally provide lower reductions and are widely used to minimize or prevent cross-contamination but show limited efficacy as a decontamination step to achieve 5-log reduction. Emerging nonthermal techniques, such as intense pulsed light and cold atmospheric plasma, demonstrate potential for pathogens reduction on pecans. Lastly, pecan shells, comprising 40%-60% of the whole nut, are rich in phenolic and flavonoid compounds with antimicrobial and antioxidant properties. Recent studies highlight their potential as natural antimicrobials, functional ingredients, and active packaging components in food safety applications. Overall, this review integrates current knowledge on contamination risks, intervention strategies, product quality, and by-product utilization for food safety in pecan production.

works.title: Synthetic sentinel microbes for in situ detection of food contaminants
Personality as a driver of food perception, preference and dietary behavior
works.abstract: Food preferences and dietary behaviours have traditionally been explained through biological determinants such as taste genetics, oral responsiveness, and cultural/environmental exposure. Growing evidence suggests that personality traits represent an important but underexplored source of individual variation in food perception and acceptance. Available studies indicate associations between personality and food-related outcomes that may involve multiple interrelated pathways. Some traits such as food neophobia, disgust sensitivity, and anxiety-related traits have been associated with responsiveness to warning-related oral sensations, and in turn to affective experience, whereas others, such as reward sensitivity and sensation seeking have primarily been associated with affective responses. Personality may also be related to behavioural tendencies that affect exposure and learning. One recent finding from a large Italian cohort suggests joint associations between personality traits and PROP responsiveness; this observation motivates a provisional psycho-sensory phenotype construct. Because most evidence is cross-sectional and several central findings await independent replication, the proposed pathways and phenotypes are presented as working hypotheses. We outline operational criteria for psycho-sensory phenotypes and discuss implications for precision nutrition, consumer-centred food innovation, and future research.
