Conventional and Emerging Protein Ingredients in Farinaceous Products: Amino Acid Quality, Digestibility, Biological Value, and Functional Performance
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: The increasing demand for protein-enriched foods has renewed interest in farinaceous products as widely consumed and technologically adaptable matrices for nutritional improvement. However, protein enrichment cannot be evaluated solely by increases in crude protein content, as nutritional value depends on essential amino acid (EAA) balance, digestibility, biological quality, technofunctional performance, bioactive potential, and interactions within the food matrix. This review critically examines the incorporation of conventional and emerging protein ingredients from animal, plant, insect, microalgal, and macroalgal sources into farinaceous systems, including flours, powders, concentrates, isolates, and hydrolysates. This review synthesizes current evidence through comparative analyses of protein content, EAA profiles, digestibility, protein digestibility-corrected amino acid score (PDCAAS), digestible indispensable amino acid score (DIAAS), technological functionality, and bioactive properties. Particular attention is given to formulation and processing strategies that improve protein quality while preserving dough or batter performance and consumer-relevant attributes. In general, the literature indicates that effective protein enrichment requires an integrated approach that combines amino acid complementation, digestibility enhancement, reduction of antinutritional constraints, technological compatibility, and sensory feasibility. This review highlights the need to move beyond protein quantity as the primary benchmark and toward multidimensional quality frameworks for designing nutritionally improved, functional, and acceptable farinaceous foods.

works.title: Tuning Meat Flavor via Cold Plasma‐Mediated Oxidation Networks: Prospects for Simultaneous Deodorization and Aroma Preservation
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: This article is the first to specifically review the flavor-oriented design of early meat products mediated by cold plasma (CP) oxidation networks. It systematically summarizes the unique mechanisms and application prospects of CP technology in regulating meat flavor and proposes that, as a nonthermal processing method, it can directly modulate lipid and protein oxidation pathways through reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS), thereby collaboratively achieving odor suppression and characteristic aroma retention. In contrast to conventional methods, CP technology precisely targets the oxidation reaction network under low-temperature conditions, thereby preventing the degradation of heat-sensitive compounds and preserving textural integrity. This approach introduces a novel strategy for the targeted design of meat flavors. Future advancements in this field will rely on elucidating the molecular interactions between CP and flavor compounds, developing integrated multi-omics analytical frameworks, and enhancing intelligent, controllable CP equipment to facilitate the technology's industrial implementation.

works.title: Research Progress, Key Challenges, and Future Prospects of Raman Spectroscopy Combined With Machine Learning in Food Analysis
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) has emerged as an important technical method for food quality and safety detection owing to its advantages, such as molecular fingerprint specificity and rapidity without damage. However, complex food matrices, susceptibility of SERS signals to fluorescence, noise, scattering interference, redundant high-dimensional spectral data, and limited model generalization ability hinder the direct application of this technique to on-site industrial detection. In recent years, machine learning (ML) and deep learning have provided revolutionary solutions for signal correction, feature extraction, qualitative and quantitative analyses, and model transfer in SERS, achieving a full-chain upgrade from data collection to intelligent analysis. This paper begins with the four-layer relationships of instrument principle, signal mechanism, algorithm logic, and food system characteristics, systematically reviews the technical paradigm of the integration of SERS and ML, analyzes the real pain points and scientific bottlenecks currently faced, and proposes future development paths from the perspectives of basic mechanisms, model interpretability, industrialization implementation, and multimodal intelligent systems, aiming to provide systematic academic references for conducting high-depth and practical SERS-ML research in the field of food science.

works.title: Cereal Biomass Valorization for Functional Food Ingredients: Fractionation and Circular Biorefinery Strategies
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Food processing must transition toward resource-efficient systems that operate within planetary boundaries. Cereals, as climate-resilient staples, offer strong potential to valorize nutrient-rich fractions. Zero-waste biorefinery concepts and green fractionation technologies, integrated with structure-function principles, enable the conversion of whole-grain biomass into functional ingredients for food applications. This review systematically evaluates recent advances in fractionation and separation technologies, including nonthermal physical and biochemical approaches. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-guided analysis of peer-reviewed articles (2020-2025) was conducted to assess extraction strategies, functional performance, and sustainability-related aspects. Mechanistic insights into recovered biopolymers are discussed to design process-functional relationships, with an emphasis on fractionation strategies such as synergistic recovery, fraction precision, and yield optimization relative to process complexity. The analysis shows that 46.75% of studies focused on common grains, whereas 53.25% utilized side streams (42.86% bran) for the recovery of proteins (32.47%), fibers (55.84%), lipids (10.39%), and phytochemicals (89.61%). Although hybrid techniques enhanced selectivity, multi-fraction recovery, and the preservation of biopolymer functionality, linear pathways dominated (70.13%), particularly in ultrasound-assisted methods (57.14%). Few studies investigated whole-system biorefinery approaches (14.29%), sustainability assessments (<5%), or pilot-scale validation (10.39%). Findings reveal critical opportunities for integrating life cycle assessment, techno-economic analysis, and digital modeling to facilitate scale-up and industrial translation. Furthermore, underutilized crops and industrial residues show promise for circular valorization. The review highlights the potential of sustainable biorefineries to reduce waste, enhance resource efficiency, and support circular-driven food innovation.

works.title: Serine protease inhibitors in legume seeds: from antinutrients towards putative gut health maintainers
works.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
works.abstract: Legume seeds contain proteins with serine protease inhibitor activity. Serine protease inhibitors (SPI) have traditionally been regarded as antinutritional compounds because of their ability to inhibit digestive serine proteases. Evidence from animal studies has demonstrated pancreatic hypertrophy following consumption of diets containing raw legume seeds and/or purified SPI, although these effects may be biased by factors such as the overall poor protein digestibility of the raw seeds. Accumulating evidence indicates that legume seed-derived SPI have anti-inflammatory activity with potential relevance to gastrointestinal health. However, the mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. This review examines current knowledge of legume seed-derived SPI in the context of both their antinutritional properties and their potential role in mitigating gut inflammation. Particular attention is given to proposed mechanisms involving SPI-mediated inhibition of neutrophil elastase, which may in turn reduce matrix metalloprotease activation and downstream inflammatory pathways. Available animal studies further suggest that a proportion of ingested SPI can remain structurally intact and biologically active in the distal intestine. Together, this evidence highlights the dual biological role of SPI and identifies key knowledge gaps, including their intestinal bioavailability and relevance to human gastrointestinal disorders.

works.title: Optimizing Water Addition to Balance Tenderness and Freeze–Thaw Stability: Processing Strategy for Tender Fish Balls
Changing Soy Protein Isolate Techno-Functional Properties via Two Cold Plasma Technologies: DBD and Glow Discharge
works.abstract: Abstract The growing demand for plant-based food systems has increased interest in non-thermal technologies that modify the functional properties of vegetable proteins without causing extensive structural damage. Among these technologies, cold plasma has emerged as a promising approach for inducing controlled structural and surface modifications in proteins. However, the effects of different plasma configurations and operational parameters on soy protein isolate (SPI) remain poorly understood. Therefore, this study investigated the effects of cold plasma treatments, using dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) and glow discharge systems, on the structural and techno-functional properties of SPI. The samples were treated at five DBD excitation frequencies (50, 250, 500, 750, and 1000 Hz) and two glow discharge gas flow rates (10 and 20 mL/min). Structural analyses included Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), while techno-functional properties included solubility, water and oil holding capacity, foaming properties, emulsion formation and stability, gel-forming ability, and hygroscopicity. The plasma treatments induced moderate structural modifications without evidence of extensive degradation of the primary protein structure. FTIR analysis revealed a reduction in β-sheet content from 57.11% in untreated SPI to 45.72% in SPI-G20, accompanied by an increase in random coil structures to 28.85%, indicating protein conformational rearrangements. These structural changes were associated with distinct techno-functional responses depending on the plasma condition. SPI-G20 exhibited the highest solubility, reaching 40.08% at pH 7, whereas SPI-D1000 showed improved gel-forming ability at lower protein concentration. Variations in foaming and emulsion-related properties were also observed, indicating that plasma treatments affected interfacial behavior and protein organization differently. Overall, the results highlight the potential of cold plasma as a versatile strategy for modulating the functional properties of SPI for specific technological applications in food systems.

works.title: Food-based dietary guidelines as policy instruments for safeguarding traditional African food systems
AI agents accelerate the discovery and engineering of food molecules
How Does Food Processing‐Induced E/Z Isomerization Regulate Carotenoid Bioaccessibility? — From Food Matrix to Mixed Micelles
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Carotenoids are essential lipophilic antioxidants in plant-derived foods, and their health benefits are highly dependent on bioaccessibility. Although carotenoids naturally occur predominantly as all-E isomers in plant tissues, food processing can induce geometrical isomerization to generate Z-isomers with enhanced bioaccessibility. This review begins by describing the accumulation, structural stability, and release of carotenoids in dietary plants and outlining key analytical methods for their detection and characterization. It then systematically summarizes the effects of thermal processing (industrial thermal sterilization, domestic cooking, and thermal drying), non-thermal processing (mechanical treatment, high-pressure processing, pulsed electric fields, ultrasonication, irradiation, non-thermal drying), and ingredient addition on carotenoid release and isomerization. Furthermore, the regulatory role of processing-induced isomeric structural changes on carotenoid bioabsorption is critically discussed. Processing alters the spatial configuration of carotenoids via E/Z isomerization, reducing crystallinity and aggregation while enhancing micellization efficiency. Concurrently, processing disrupts the plant matrix, promoting the release of isomerized products, thereby improving bioaccessibility. The effects on isomerization degree and bioaccessibility vary with processing method and parameters: moderate processing favors Z-isomer formation, whereas excessive processing leads to degradation. Elucidating the mechanisms of processing-induced E/Z isomerization and its regulation on bioaccessibility provides a theoretical basis for the scientific processing of plant-derived foods and precision nutrition, offering new perspectives for integrating food processing technology and nutritional science.

works.title: Coconut Waste as a Functional Platform for Biopolymer‐Based Food Packaging Films: A Comprehensive Review
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Petroleum-based plastic packaging has led to severe environmental concerns, whereas biopolymer films, despite their sustainability, often suffer from limited mechanical strength, poor moisture resistance, and insufficient functional activity. Coconut by-products represent an abundant and renewable resource with significant potential to address these limitations and support circular economy strategies in food packaging. This review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of recent advances in coconut-based functionalized biopolymer films, systematically covering the sources, extraction, and modification of key coconut-derived materials, including cellulose, coconut oil, polyphenol-rich extracts, and coconut proteins. A structure-property-function perspective is adopted to elucidate how these components influence the mechanical, barrier, and functional performance of composite films. Coconut nanocellulose serves as an effective reinforcing phase, enhancing mechanical strength, barrier properties, and thermal stability, while also enabling active and intelligent packaging functionalities. Coconut oil improves hydrophobicity, flexibility, and antimicrobial activity, although its compatibility with hydrophilic matrices remains a key challenge. Polyphenol-rich extracts impart antioxidant and antifungal properties and, in anthocyanin-rich systems, enable pH-responsive colorimetric sensing. Coconut proteins exhibit intrinsic film-forming capability and contribute to structural integrity. Overall performance is strongly governed by component selection, interfacial compatibility, and compositional balance within multicomponent systems. However, key challenges remain, including raw material variability, instability of bioactive compounds, limited scalability, and concerns regarding migration safety. Future research should focus on interfacial engineering, stabilization of multicomponent systems, and the development of scalable processing strategies to facilitate practical applications in sustainable food packaging.

works.title: Carbon Catabolite Repression and Quorum Sensing Interplay in Marine Fish Spoilage: An Integrated Metabolic Perspective
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Bacterial quorum sensing (QS) systems pose a significant challenge to the preservation of protein-rich marine fish, as coordinated spoilage behaviors such as biofilm formation and volatile amine production are activated under specific metabolic conditions. Despite well-characterized spoilage organisms, the regulatory logic linking metabolic state to QS-driven collective behaviors remains incompletely understood. Thus, the goals of this review were to synthesize current knowledge on how carbon catabolite repression (CCR) gates QS-dependent spoilage programs in marine fish; examine the molecular mechanisms by which global regulators (cAMP-CRP, Crc/CrcZ, CcpA, (p)ppGpp-RpoS) interface with QS circuitry; and describe how this mechanistic understanding can be translated into anti-virulence preservation strategies that mislead metabolic sensors or disrupt quorum communication. In particular, this review focuses on the ecological manifestations of CCR-QS crosstalk in key spoilage genera and the latest progress in integrating metabolic modulators with QS inhibitors within stimuli-responsive smart packaging. Finally, current challenges limiting the systematic application of this metabolic perspective in the fish industry are discussed, including unresolved molecular interfaces in nonmodel spoilage organisms and methodological bottlenecks in spatially resolved analysis. It is important to note that while the proposed CCR-QS framework is strongly supported by direct mechanistic evidence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, its molecular details remain largely unvalidated in most major marine fish specific spoilage organisms (SSOs). Nevertheless, this framework offers a testable conceptual scaffold that integrates nutrient-driven growth kinetics with QS-mediated social behavior, providing a mechanistic basis for designing next-generation precision preservation strategies.

works.title: Microwave-Ultrasound Binary Extraction Process (MUBEP): A Green Method for Extraction of Polyphenols from Pomegranate Peel Biomass
works.abstract: Abstract Pomegranate peel (PP) biomass, which is rich in bioactive phytochemicals, is one of the more intriguing agro-food byproducts. Microwave-Ultrasound Binary Extraction Process (MUBEP) was performed for extraction of polyphenols. A Box-Behnken design was used to investigate the effects of process variables on extraction efficacy. The optimized process conditions, including 400 W microwave power, 10 min microwave time, and 9 min ultrasonication, resulted in 73.6% yield, 3460.67 mg/L GAE total phenolics content, 291 mg C3G/g anthocyanin content, 30.71 mg QE/g total flavonoids, 264.13 mg TE/g reducing power, 75.279% DPPH, and 63.788 mg AAE/100 ml FRAP in dry pomegranate peel. All responses possessing a quadratic model were significantly validated with a regression coefficient (R²) above 0.95. The FTIR spectroscopy and UHPLC-MS reveal the presence of polyphenols in the obtained extract. This research proposes the development of novel and environmentally friendly MUBEP techniques to enhance the extraction of polyphenols from pomegranate peel biomass

works.title: Integrated metabolomic and transcriptomic analysis of oligoproanthocyanidins biotransformation by rhizosphere filamentous fungi from tea plant (Camellia sinensis)
works.abstract: Incomplete degradation of proanthocyanidins (PAs) causes astringency, reduces nutrient bioavailability in foods, and hinders the feed use of agricultural residues, posing a critical challenge to the food industry. Herein, we explored the potential of tea plant rhizospheric fungi from long-term PAs-enriched habitats to degrade oligoproanthocyanidins (OPC). The five isolated fungal strains were capable of utilizing OPC as a carbon source and exhibited growth comparable to that observed in sucrose-based media. Under submerged fermentation, these fungi metabolized OPC, resulting in changes in pH and color that served as indicators. This process yielded eight fungal metabolites with nutritional and antibacterial properties, notably schizostatin, which was produced by the edible mushroom Schizophyllum commune ScCYS1063. Non-targeted metabolomics revealed that OPC degradation was linked to central energy metabolic pathways. Furthermore, transcriptomic analysis indicated the pattern of PAs as a carbon source capable of fueling fumagillin biosynthesis, triggering class-level transcriptional responses of genes encoding monooxygenases, cytochrome P450S, and dioxygenases. Recovered extracellular proteins effectively degraded procyanidin B2, supporting the potential for controlled enzymatic processes to break down OPC. This study highlights the value of harnessing microbial communities from tea rhizosphere to advance biotransformation of natural metabolites, offering novel solutions for the food industry.

works.title: From aroma cue to feeding behavior: Sichuan pepper essential oil aroma stimulates appetite via cognitive and physiological pathways
works.abstract: Abstract Reduced food intake is a key contributor to malnutrition. The sense of smell plays a fundamental role in appetite regulation, and olfactory stimulation with certain spice essential oils can facilitate oral intake. The present study examined three Sichuan pepper (genus Zanthoxylum) essential oil (SPEO) types by assessing their effects on self-reported appetite ( n = 348) and ad libitum food intake ( n = 78) in humans, and on feeding behavior and hypothalamic neuropeptide expression in mice. In humans, exposure to SPEO aromas enhanced general appetite and modulated sensory-specific appetite, and increased total food intake by 15–19% in male participants with a shift toward salty foods. This effect was more pronounced in frequent consumers, supporting a learned, cognitive pathway. Concurrently, in mice, SPEO inhalation significantly promoted acute food intake, which was closely associated with altered mRNA expression profiles of hypothalamic feeding-related neuropeptides (upregulating MCH and orexin, downregulating POMC). Further analysis identified five appetite-enhancing volatile compounds (β-Phellandrene, Linalool, Ocimene, Eucalyptol, Linalyl acetate). Collectively, these findings support the appetite-promoting effect of SPEO aroma and suggest that this effect involves both convergent cognitive and physiological pathways.

works.title: Spatially structured food fermentation: Integrating matrix transport, microbial function, and predictive modeling
works.abstract: Background Food fermentation emerges from dynamic interactions between microbial metabolism and the physicochemical structure of food matrices. Although starter cultures have improved process control, microbial performance cannot be understood independently of the environment in which microorganisms grow. In structured, semi-solid, and solid foods, limitations in heat and mass transfer generate spatially heterogeneous microenvironments characterized by gradients in temperature, oxygen, pH, water activity, nutrients, and metabolites. These local conditions can influence microbial physiology, metabolic activity, interactions, and community development, while microbial activity progressively modifies the surrounding matrix. Scope and approach This review develops a matrix-aware framework for understanding and predicting food fermentation by integrating microbial ecology, matrix properties, transport phenomena, and predictive modeling. Evidence from dairy, meat, cereal, plant-based, and solid-state fermentations is examined to describe how matrix composition, structure, porosity, hydration, and process geometry regulate heat, gas, moisture, substrate, and metabolite transport and thereby determine the local physicochemical conditions experienced by microorganisms. Particular attention is given to the connection between these microenvironments and microbial responses, from metabolic regulation to population interactions and community dynamics. Mechanistic kinetic, reaction–diffusion, heat- and mass-transfer models are evaluated together with emerging approaches integrating spatial measurements, sensors, omics, machine learning, and hybrid modeling. Experimental studies are also considered to illustrate how transport limitations and matrix properties translate into measurable heterogeneity in real fermentation systems. Key findings and conclusions The available evidence indicates that bulk process variables can mask substantial spatial and temporal heterogeneity within structured foods, meaning that microorganisms located within the same fermentation system may experience markedly different physicochemical conditions. Microbial functionality therefore reflects not only intrinsic metabolic capacity or starter identity, but also the ability of the food matrix to transport heat, gases, water, nutrients, and metabolites. This relationship is bidirectional: microbial growth, substrate conversion, acidification, gas and metabolite production, heat generation, and structural changes continuously reshaping the matrix and its transport properties. A matrix-aware approach consequently provides a mechanistic bridge between food structure, local microenvironment, microbial function, community dynamics, and fermentation outcomes. Combining spatially resolved measurements with mechanistic and data-driven models could improve starter culture selection, process prediction, scale-up, and control while reducing reliance on empirical optimization. Such integration may support more consistent and resource-efficient fermentation processes, particularly for structured foods, emerging plant-based products, and the valorization of food side-streams.

Recent Advances in Microbial Community Composition of Fermented Soy Whey and Its Mechanism for Biotransformation of Soybean Isoflavones
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Fermented soy whey (FSW), a traditional natural tofu coagulant, harbors complex microbial communities that drive soy-protein coagulation via organic-acid secretion and enhance the bioavailability of soybean isoflavones, conferring desirable flavor characteristics and health-beneficial bioactivities. However, several critical knowledge gaps restrict its scaled-up industrial deployment. The dynamic regulatory connections between microbial community temporal succession and metabolite biosynthesis during spontaneous FSW fermentation have not been fully deciphered. Interspecies interactions inside highly heterogeneous microbial consortia remain ambiguous, and the whole-fermentation system is exceptionally sensitive to fluctuating environmental conditions. This review synthesizes prior literature together with cutting-edge multi-omics datasets to systematically dissect the temporal dynamics of FSW microbial ecosystems. Enzymatic mechanistic analysis delineates key catalytic and metabolic pathways responsible for transforming soy isoflavone glucosides into aglycones and subsequent bioactive derivatives. We critically evaluate promising technical strategies, covering targeted synthetic-biology modification, integrated intelligent control systems, artificial intelligence, and digital-twin modeling, to advance the transition from experience-driven spontaneous fermentation to precision manufacturing. Selective manipulation of functional microbes or rate-limiting catalytic enzymes enables directional enrichment of high-activity isoflavone metabolites. This framework mitigates bioavailability drawbacks of native isoflavones and builds solid scientific foundations for zero-waste valorization of soy-processing by-products, circular food manufacturing, and innovative high-value-added functional-food development.

Interplay of printability, swallowing safety, and nutrient bioaccessibility in 3D-printed biopolymer hydrogels for texture-modified diets
works.abstract: : Background Extrusion-based 3D/4D printing of biopolymer hydrogels is increasingly explored to develop texture-modified diets for individuals with swallowing difficulties and elevated nutritional risk. Key objectives include maintaining structural integrity, swallowing safety, and adequate nutrient delivery. While higher hydrocolloid concentration and increased network density improve printability and swallowing safety, clinical evidence suggests these modifications may compromise nutrient release. This gap remains largely unaddressed in food-printing research. Scope and approach Applying a PRISMA 2020-guided search (January 2022-July 2026; ScienceDirect, Scopus, Web of Science) and a uniform three-axis extraction schema, 129 primary studies on printable hydrogels, emulsion gels, high-internal-phase emulsions and bigels for texture-modified or dysphagia-oriented foods were analyzed. Printability, swallowing safety, and nutrient bioaccessibility were extracted against shared formulation variables to assess their interdependence, rather than optimizing them individually. Key findings and conclusions Findings show that increasing network density and viscosity improves print quality and swallowing safety but, in most matrices, restricts nutrient release; when a nutrient is carried in a discrete, protected phase, higher density can instead enhance bioaccessibility, so the pattern is not universal. No study measured intake. Only 12 of 129 studies (9.3%; 95% CI 5.4–15.6%) measured printability, safety, and nutrition together, highlighting a research gap. Five strategies can balance these outcomes: phase separation, modified print geometry, networks that disintegrate after swallowing, nutrient-rich ingredients instead of purified hydrocolloids, and reaction-based texturization. Data remain limited on biocompatibility, tribology, safety in older adults, and sensory effects. A minimum reporting set is proposed to improve comparability.

works.title: Upcycling agri-food by-products into redox-active ingredients for skeletal muscle health: From processing chemistry to human translation
works.abstract: Background Agri-food processing generates chemically complex side streams that retain polyphenols, carotenoids, tocopherols, minerals, and fermentable fiber. Their valorization is attractive for functional-food innovation; however, experimental characterization often emphasizes chemical antioxidant assays, which alone do not establish biological efficacy or substantiate a skeletal-muscle health claim. Scope and Approach This critical review connects food-side-stream chemistry and processing with skeletal-muscle redox physiology, bioavailability, microbiota metabolism, human evidence, safety, sensory design, and sustainability. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing direct evidence from authenticated by-product ingredients from supportive evidence from compositionally related whole-food preparations. Key Findings and Conclusions Contracting muscle requires physiological ROS/RNS for Nrf2-, AMPK/MAPK-, and PGC-1α-dependent adaptation; therefore, successful ingredients should normalize excess oxidant damage without extinguishing adaptive signaling. Grape seed/pomace, pomegranate peel/press residues, berry pomaces, citrus peels, cereal brans, coffee silverskin, and related side streams contain plausible redox-active compounds, but clinical substantiation is uneven. Meta-analyses of polyphenol-rich foods show modest improvements in recovery outcomes (standardized mean differences of 0.23–0.50 for recovery of maximal isometric force between 0 and 96 h), while recent trials with the microbiota-derived ellagitannin metabolite urolithin A provide a mechanistically coherent example of mitochondrial translation; nevertheless, free urolithin A circulates at low-nanomolar concentrations, about three orders of magnitude below the concentrations used to induce mitophagy in vitro. No randomized trial of an authenticated, standardized by-product ingredient with a muscle endpoint (Tier I) was identified. The major bottleneck is not discovering antioxidant-rich biomass but reproducibly converting heterogeneous residues into chemically defined, safe, bioavailable, and consumer-acceptable ingredients. A farm-to-function framework integrating traceability, metabolomics, green extraction, pharmacokinetics, randomized trials, life-cycle assessment, and regulatory substantiation is proposed for the next generation of muscle-health functional foods.

Soy isoflavones in cancer: molecular pathways, pharmacokinetic constraints and translational opportunities
works.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
works.abstract: Soy isoflavones are dietary phytoestrogens that have attracted considerable interest in cancer prevention and integrative oncology because of their ability to interact with estrogen receptor signaling and multiple cancer-related molecular networks. Researchers have investigated the major soy-derived isoflavones, particularly genistein, daidzein, and glycitein, across experimental, epidemiological, and clinical settings. Preclinical evidence indicates that these compounds can modulate key processes involved in tumor initiation and progression, including cell-cycle regulation, apoptosis, oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling, angiogenesis, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and epigenetic regulation. These effects appear to involve coordinated regulation of ER, PI3K/Akt/mTOR, MAPK, Wnt/β-catenin, NF-κB, TGF-β, Nrf2, and non-coding RNA-associated networks, supporting their role as context-dependent biological modulators rather than conventional cytotoxic agents. Epidemiological studies generally report modest inverse associations between soy intake and selected malignancies, particularly breast and prostate cancers, although findings vary by tumor type, population, diet, and exposure assessment. Clinical translation remains constrained by discrepancies between in vitro exposure conditions and human pharmacokinetics, since circulating isoflavones occur mainly as glucuronide and sulfate conjugates with limited free aglycone exposure. Microbiota-dependent equol production further contributes to interindividual variability. This review synthesizes molecular, pharmacokinetic, metabolic, and translational evidence, positioning soy isoflavones as chemopreventive or adjunctive modulators requiring biomarker-guided clinical validation.

works.title: Food and packaging applications of black soldier fly larvae fractions: from processing and functionality to safety and consumer acceptance
works.abstract: Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) provide multiple processing-defined fractions for food and food-contact applications. This review evaluates four major fractions: (1) proteins for nutritional and techno-functional applications, (2) lipids for formulation, (3) peptide-rich fractions with candidate bioactivities, and (4) chitin/chitosan for food-contact materials. Protein fractions have the broadest direct food application evidence, while translation requires food safety validation and consumer evaluation across sensory response stated willingness and indirect food pathways.

works.title: Comprehensive characterization of shilajit from varied provenance: elemental profile, urolithin A content, and antimicrobial activity
works.abstract: Shilajit is an exudate rich in humic substances that collected from rocks in several mountain ranges and has been used for centuries in traditional medicine for fatigue, physical performance, and general vitality. Ten shilajit samples from five mountain regions (Himalayas, Andes, Altai, Caucasus, and Carpathians) were assessed by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), elemental composition by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), urolithin A (Uro-A) content by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), and antimicrobial activity by broth microdilution against five bacterial and five fungal species. DSC identified two distinct thermal groups: seven samples showed only melting transitions between 100–159 °C, while three samples exhibited low-temperature crystallization and sub-zero melting. ICP-MS revealed potassium as the dominant macroelement (up to ~95,600 ppm), with essential trace elements (selenium, zinc and iron) and toxic elements [arsenic (0.14–1.34 ppm), cadmium (0.01–0.10 ppm) and lead (0.35–3.01 ppm)] all present at levels well within FDA/WHO tolerable intake thresholds, comparable to background levels reported in common foods such as dark chocolate. Uro-A content was strongly solvent-dependent, ranging from 0.07 to 1.63 ppm in methanol to 3.46–58.46 ppm in a methanol/ethyl acetate mixture. Antimicrobial activity was species-dependent (MIC 3.12–25 mg/mL), limited to Bacillus subtilis and Staphylococcus aureus and only two fungal strains ( Mucor mucedo and Geotrichum candidum ), with no activity against the Escherichia coli and Proteus mirabilis . These findings support shilajit’s compositional diversity and highlight Uro-A as its most promising bioactive component, warranting further standardization and origin-based sourcing studies for future bioavailability studies for the potential use as a functional food ingredient.

works.title: Light-vibration synergy during spreading and optimized drying temperature improve machine-harvested beverage-grade green tea quality
works.abstract: Optimizing the flavor profile of machine-harvested beverage-grade green tea requires a delicate balance between the retention of low-boiling-point volatiles and the progression of thermal reactions. This study demonstrates that a synergistic light-vibration pretreatment combined with drying at 75 °C is a superior strategy to address this challenge. Using quantitative descriptive analysis (QDA), headspace solid-phase microextraction-gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (HS-SPME-GC-MS), and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), we found that this protocol significantly elevated the total volatile emission to 20301.17 μg/kg. Crucially, it shifted the compositional profile toward esters and terpenes, which serve as the primary contributors to the floral and fruity notes of green tea. A total of 101 volatile compounds were identified, and nine key aroma-active constituents were screened out. These findings not only elucidate the metabolic pathways activated by light-vibration synergy but also provide a scalable and implementable technical solution for the industrial production of high-aroma, machine-harvested beverage-grade green teas.

works.title: Sustainable postharvest vegetable disease management: integrating physiological insights and innovative technologies for quality preservation
works.abstract: Abstract This review summarizes the underlying causes of postharvest diseases in key vegetable crops and describes novel control strategies including biocontrol, natural antimicrobials, physical treatments, and innovative packaging technologies. A sustainable Integrated Postharvest Disease Management (IPDM) approach is proposed, based on overlapping preventive methods designed to reduce postharvest losses and maintain produce quality. The practical value of multi-omic analyses in elucidating mechanisms of pathogenicity and host resistance is also discussed.

works.title: Association of chrono-nutrition behaviors with cognitive function in middle-aged and older adults
works.abstract: Chrono-nutrition, as a new branch of nutritional science, examines the health implications of meal timing, frequency, regularity and its coordination with circadian rhythms. Emerging studies highlight the pivotal role of chrono-nutrition behaviors on aging, yet the associations with cognitive function remain inconclusive. Information on chrono-nutrition behaviors was assessed using validated questionnaires. The global and domain-specific cognition were evaluated using a battery of neuropsychological tests. Linear and logistic regression models were employed to assess the associations. False discovery rates (FDRs) were controlled using multiple-comparison corrections. Greater eating frequency and snacks were associated with worse global cognition and poorer memory. With respect to meal timing, nighttime eating ( β = −0.21, 95% CI: −0.33 ~ −0.09, FDR- P = 0.004) and prolonged eating windows ( β = −0.29, 95% CI: −0.38 ~ −0.21, FDR- P < 0.001) were significantly related to worse memory. Regarding the coordination of eating with circadian rhythms, longer morning latency was associated with worse global and attention, whereas longer evening latency was prominently related to better global cognition and memory function ( β = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.19 ~ 0.38, FDR- P < 0.001). Chrono-nutrition behaviors characterized by higher eating frequency, more snacks, nighttime eating, extended eating windows, longer morning latency, and shorter evening latency were associated with poorer cognition, particularly memory function. These findings underscore the importance of chrono-nutrition in cognitive health.

works.title: The global potential of aquavoltaics for power generation and offsetting the carbon footprint of freshwater aquaculture
works.abstract: Abstract Rising pressures at the energy–food–climate nexus are driving demand for more sustainable production systems. Global inland freshwater aquaculture has rapidly expanded, intensifying greenhouse gas emissions and sustainability challenges. As a potential solution, aquavoltaics—integrating photovoltaics with aquaculture—offers multifunctional benefits, but its global deployment and decarbonization potential remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate satellite observation products with realistic climate-driven photovoltaic system simulations to map the global expansion patterns and installation potential of aquavoltaics. The results revealed a current global aquavoltaics area of 423 km2 by 2023, with China accounting for the overwhelming majority (97%). We estimate that deploying PV with a 40% coverage rate across over 50,000 km² of landside clustering of aquaculture ponds globally could yield an electricity generation potential of 4,143 ± 145 TWh yr-1, sufficient to support energy self-sufficiency in many cities and offset freshwater aquaculture carbon footprint in numerous countries. These findings highlight aquavoltaics as a scalable pathway towards sustainable aquaculture and low-carbon energy futures.

works.title: Conflict with industrial fleets undermines the contributions of small-scale fisheries to sustainable development in vulnerable regions
works.abstract: Equitable and sustainable governance of small-scale fisheries (SSFs) is essential for achieving food security and conservation in coastal areas. Yet in increasingly industrialized oceans, competition and conflict with large-scale fisheries (LSFs) threaten the contributions of SSFs to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Here we have developed a small-scale and industrial fisheries interaction index and applied it to 126 countries using 2 recent global datasets. Vulnerability to conflict is highest in countries where SSFs are vital for nutrition, but governance is weak, especially in Africa, Oceania and Asia. We also identify low-exposure outlier countries with unexpectedly low risk of SSF–LSF interactions, providing insights for proactive policy. Preferential access areas granting spatial rights to SSFs are common in both low- and high-vulnerability countries, suggesting such policies are often reactive and may be insufficient alone without strong enforcement. As ocean industries expand, it will be necessary to strengthen SSF access rights and limit LSF overcapacity to reduce conflict and advance sustainable development. Small-scale fisheries are vulnerable to conflict with industrial fishing. The small-scale and industrial fisheries interaction index reveals regions with weak governance and emphasizes the need for enhanced access rights and management strategies.

works.title: Advanced Functional Packaging Strategies for Postharvest Fruit Preservation: From Physiological Regulation to Intelligent Monitoring
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: ABSTRACT Postharvest fruits are highly susceptible to rapid senescence and microbial decay, a process primarily driven by intense respiration and endogenous ethylene signaling. While conventional packaging provides basic physical protection, the shift towards multi‐component functional interfaces offers dynamic solutions for physiological regulation. This review provides a critical analysis of advanced functional packaging strategies, focusing on the synergistic integration of natural biopolymers, deep eutectic solvents (DESs), and nanoporous structures. We dissect the intrinsic mechanisms by which these materials modulate the microenvironment dynamics, particularly the precise control of O 2 /CO 2 /C 2 H 4 fluxes and moisture migration, and their impact on fruit oxidative stress markers and metabolic pathways. Furthermore, we evaluate the feasibility of transitioning from passive barriers to stimulus‐responsive intelligent systems, highlighting the convergence of flexible sensors, radio frequency identification (RFID) data acquisition, and machine‐learning models that together enable real‐time quality monitoring throughout the supply chain. Finally, we analyze the trade‐off between the large‐scale application of bio‐based materials and the precision of active ingredient release, and further highlight how divergent regulatory frameworks for food‐contact materials in major markets (e.g., the European Union, the United States, and China) constrain industrial application. Based on the collaborative assessment of the above‐mentioned technical and institutional bottlenecks, differentiated breakthrough paths have been discussed to provide a roadmap for the development of sustainable, high‐performance preservation technologies after harvest.

Valorization of yak bone collagen byproducts: computational screening and experimental validation of anti-aging peptides targeting MMP-1
works.abstract: Abstract Valorization of yak collagen byproducts offers a sustainable route to food-derived bioactive peptides. To prioritize candidate peptides from yak collagen-derived sequences, we developed AgeAttnMLP, an ESM-2-based screening model that achieved an AUC of 0.891 under conventional five-fold cross-validation and 0.879 under an additional cluster-aware grouped evaluation. Screening of yak collagen sequences followed by Alcalase-guided in silico hydrolysis identified TGPPGPSGI, GEPGAPGE, and GPSGEPGTA as lead candidates. GEPGAPGE showed the strongest MMP-1 inhibition, with an IC 50 of 126 μg/mL. Molecular dynamics simulations and MM-PBSA analysis suggested that peptide binding destabilized the β-sheet spanning residues 76–78 near the catalytic region, potentially affecting substrate recognition. Under the tested conditions, all three peptides extended the lifespan of Caenorhabditis elegans, with the greatest effect observed for GPSGEPGTA at 7.5 mg/mL. These findings establish an integrated computational–experimental strategy for discovering collagen-derived peptides and support the value-added utilization of yak collagen byproducts as potential functional food ingredients.

Nova was never built for the populations it claims to protect
works.abstract: The Nova classification system has achieved remarkable global traction as the primary instrument for identifying ultra-processed foods in research and dietary policy. Yet the populations Nova purports to protect, those most exposed to food-industry expansion, least able to access alternatives and most burdened by diet-related disease, may be those for whom the framework is least suitable. Nova’s Group 4 designation relies on culturally specific and operationally imprecise criteria that elevate the culinary norms of high-income, food-secure populations into a framework presented as universally applicable. The resulting classification cannot be applied consistently, produces regulatory proposals that cannot be consistently enforced, and generates guidance that is often difficult to implement in the populations most affected by diet-related disease. This Perspective argues that Nova, as currently constituted, is best suited to populations with the resources to act on its recommendations and that progress will require either a more rigorous and reproducible successor framework or clearer recognition of the limits of the current one.

works.title: When do starch–polyphenol complexes qualify as type 5 resistant starch? A critical evidence framework from molecular assembly to colonic utilization
works.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
works.abstract: Starch-polyphenol complexes are increasingly explored for modulating starch digestibility, developing low-glycemic-index foods, and improving polyphenol stability and delivery. Some systems have been described as type 5 resistant starch (RS5) or RS5-like based on V-type crystalline signals, increased resistant starch content, or reduced glucose release. However, these outcomes alone are insufficient for RS5 assignment because they may also arise from surface adsorption, non-inclusion networks, substrate shielding, enzyme inhibition by free or released polyphenols, or food-matrix effects. This review critically assesses the evidence required to describe starch-polyphenol systems as V-type starch-polyphenol complexes with demonstrated enzymatic resistance and examines their relationship to the proposed non-lipid extension of RS5. Evidence from molecular assembly, structural characterization, processing-induced rearrangement, resistance to enzymatic digestion, polyphenol release, colonic fermentation, and physiological relevance is integrated. V-type or V-type-like inclusion provides the strongest structural basis for identifying a V-type starch-polyphenol complex, whereas surface-bound complexes, non-inclusion networks and covalent derivatives require different mechanistic descriptions. Mechanistic attribution should include removal and quantification of unbound polyphenols, physical-mixture and washed-complex controls, and enzyme-inhibition kinetics. A tiered evidence framework is proposed to classify these systems as putative RS5, RS5-like complexes, polyphenol-bound resistant starch candidates, enzyme-inhibition-dominated systems, or non-RS mixtures.

works.title: Macrofungal pigments as sustainable food and nutraceutical ingredients: chemical diversity, biosynthesis, functionality, and product development
works.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
works.abstract: Pigments are widely used in food, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries, but concerns over the toxicity, environmental persistence, and ecological risks of synthetic dyes have increased demand for safe and sustainable natural alternatives. Macrofungi are promising pigment sources because of their species diversity, distinctive secondary metabolism, and potential for controlled cultivation or fermentation. Their pigments include carotenoids, quinones, melanins, and polyphenolic compounds, many of which have been associated with antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer-related activities. Compared with many plant-derived pigments, macrofungal pigments may reduce dependence on seasonal and geographical factors and support standardized production. However, practical application remains constrained by low or unstable yields, pigment degradation, incomplete structural characterization, limited validation in real food matrices, and insufficient safety and quality specifications. This review summarizes the chemical classes, biosynthetic features, structure-function relationships, extraction and stabilization strategies, biological activities, and food applications of macrofungal pigments. More importantly, this review outlines an application-oriented evaluation framework that links pigment identity, ingredient form, matrix compatibility, bioaccessibility, safety assessment, quality specifications, and intended product use, providing a critical basis for transforming macrofungal pigments from colored extracts into defined food and nutraceutical ingredients.

Whole-genome sequencing reveals clonal connectivity of Listeria monocytogenes across hygienically separated processing lines in a fresh-cut produce facility
works.abstract: Listeria monocytogenes control in fresh-cut produce facilities relies heavily on hygienic zoning and physical segregation of processing lines, under the assumption that these measures limit microbiological connectivity between compartments. However, whether segregated lines within a single facility harbour genomically independent populations has rarely been assessed at high resolution. Here, we investigated the population structure and connectivity of L . monocytogenes in two physically and hygienically segregated processing lines (cut-fruit and cut-lettuce) within a fresh-cut produce facility. Whole-genome sequencing was performed on 100 isolates collected during three pre-sanitation sampling campaigns. High-quality assemblies were analysed using multilocus sequence typing (MLST), core-genome MLST (cgMLST) and high-quality SNP (hqSNP) approaches. The population was dominated by two sequence types, ST155 (81%) and ST6 (19%), both displaying limited intra-lineage diversity consistent with closely related clonal populations (median pairwise distances of 7 and 3 hqSNPs, respectively). Hygienic compartmentalization did not result in genomically independent populations. Within each lineage, processing line accounted for only a minor fraction of genomic variation, between-line genetic distances were comparable to within-line distances, and near-identical genotypes were recovered from both lines. Two distinct connectivity patterns were identified: a facility-wide distribution of ST155, with boot-washer and floor isolates clustering across lines, consistent with transfer through personnel-associated routes; and a more localized, drain-associated connectivity pattern involving ST6. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that hygienic segregation alone does not ensure microbiological independence between processing lines and highlight the importance of monitoring hygienic transition zones, including footwear sanitation stations, mobile equipment and drainage systems.

Quantitative lipidomics reveals differences in oil metabolism and nutritional profiles of soybeans with various seed coat colors
works.abstract: Abstract Soybean seeds are rich in high-quality lipids. However, the oil content, differential metabolic pathways, and nutritional characteristics of soybeans with different seed coat colors remain unclear. In this study, the oil content of 169 soybean accessions, including yellow, green, brown, and black soybeans, was determined using the Soxhlet extraction. The results revealed a negative association between oil content and seed coat pigmentation, with yellow seeds exhibiting the highest oil content and black seeds the lowest. Metabolomic analysis of two representative accessions from each seed coat color group showed that lipid subclasses were consistently involved in the significantly altered metabolic pathways across soybean color groups. Subsequent quantitative lipidomic profiling of the 8 accessions identified 650 lipid species belonging to 5 major classes and 26 subclasses. HPLC quantification further showed that total lipid content decreased progressively with increasing seed coat pigmentation, mainly due to changes in triglycerides (TGs), phosphatidylethanolamines (PEs), phosphatidylcholines (PCs), and phosphatidylinositols (PIs). In addition, 38 differentially accumulated lipids were identified between common yellow and black soybeans, and these lipids were significantly enriched in the sphingolipid metabolism pathway. Overall, this study elucidates the relationship between soybean seed coat color and oil composition, providing a potential scientific basis for the functional utilization and dietary application of different color soybeans.

works.title: AI-guided discovery of fungal-derived salty and saltiness-enhancing peptides for sodium-reduced foods
works.abstract: Natural salty and saltiness-enhancing peptides are promising candidates for sodium reduction in food systems. This study established an integrated AI-guided workflow combining in silico hydrolysis, embedding-based machine learning, electronic tongue validation, cellular evaluation, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulation to identify fungal-derived saltiness-modulating peptides. A taste-active peptide dataset was constructed, and Uni-Mol, ESM-3, and MolCLR embeddings were compared using the same FT-Transformer framework. ESM-3 showed the most favorable classification performance and was selected for screening peptides generated from 14 fungal proteomes. Six candidates were synthesized, including the salty peptides AGHQR, AHDQY, and SKPGNR, and the saltiness-enhancing peptides IPVVVDL, DNNEEW, and ANSDL. Electronic tongue analysis identified AHDQY as the strongest salty peptide in deionized water and ANSDL as the most effective saltiness enhancer in a low-salt NaCl system. These peptides exhibited good cytocompatibility and protected HUVECs against high-salt-induced cellular injury to varying degrees, as evidenced by restored nitric oxide (NO) production and reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations further supported their stable interactions with the transmembrane channel-like protein 4 (TMC4) and peptide-induced modulation of local receptor flexibility and secondary structure. These findings provide promising fungal-derived peptide candidates and a systematic strategy for developing natural saltiness-modulating ingredients for sodium-reduced foods.

works.title: Tea Microbiomes and Metabolic Transformations From Fresh Leaf to Fermentation and Gut: Implications for Quality and Health
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Microbiomes influence tea quality, safety, and health from production to consumption, yet most studies and reviews examine individual stages. This review uses the Tea Plant-Fermentation-Gut Continuum to assess cross-stage microbial and metabolic connectivity, not as an established transmission chain. It separates microbial origin and persistence from processing-associated chemical transformation and host responses. At the leaf-to-processing interface, phyllosphere and endophytic communities may contribute to the processing microbial pool, but taxonomic overlap does not demonstrate directional transmission, and strain-level persistence remains unproven. During processing, plant enzymes and microbial activities shape tea chemistry differently across tea types, affecting pigment and aroma development. At the processing-to-gut interface, current evidence mainly supports chemical and metabolic continuity: tea- and fermentation-derived compounds reach the gut and are metabolized by resident microbiota, whereas evidence that fermentation-associated microorganisms survive, persist, or colonize the gut remains insufficient. These metabolites are linked to FXR-FGF15, AMPK, and AhR signaling and to metabolic, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective effects, mostly in preclinical models; human evidence remains limited. Together, the evidence does not support an uninterrupted microbial transmission pathway across these stages. Key gaps remain in microbial origin, persistence, activity, causality, and host relevance. Shared taxa may reflect persistence, environmental acquisition, or compositional overlap rather than direct transmission; tea type, cultivar, processing, dose, and host microbiota limit generalization. Strain-resolved tracking, controlled experiments, functional omics, and metabolic tracing are needed to distinguish association from persistence, activity, and causal function. Addressing these gaps will support evidence-based tea processing, precision fermentation, and microbiome-informed nutrition.

Computational refinement for structural identification of catechins and oxidation products in Chinese black tea
works.abstract: Characterization of natural products and their metabolites in foods is hindered by isomeric ambiguity, limited authentic standards, and compounds absent from libraries. Here, this study presents a confidence-stratified identification workflow adapted from Metabolomics Standards Initiative (MSI) Levels 1–4, spanning standard-confirmed identification, putative annotation, tentative structural or class assignment, and pathway-supported characterization of unknowns. Using UHPLC-QTOF, the workflow was applied to catechins and their oxidation products in Chinese black tea. 27 compounds were confirmed at MSI Level 1 using an in-house library, while 16 oxidation products were annotated at Level 2 by integrating public libraries with SIRIUS-based formula prediction, structure ranking, and class annotation. For compounds absent from libraries, a pathway-informed in-silico pipeline constrained structural space and enabled tentative annotation at MSI Levels 3–4. The approach was further exemplified using oxidation products of theasinensin A and theaflavic acid, reducing the number of chemically plausible candidates for these unknown features.

works.title: Banana starch nanoparticles exacerbate colitis by impairing intestinal barrier integrity in mice
works.abstract: The safety of foodborne nanoparticles has attracted significant attention in recent years. Previous studies have shown that banana-derived starch nanoparticles (BSNs) can disrupt intestinal barrier function and induce low-grade colitis in healthy mice. However, the in vivo role of these BSNs in intestinal inflammation remains unclear. Here, we show that oral exposure to BSNs aggravated the condition of the mice with DSS-induced colitis. Specifically, BSNs shortened colon length, elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, and exacerbated intestinal barrier damage in mice with colitis. Mechanistic studies revealed that BSNs exacerbated the impairment of tight junction structure and the imbalance of gut microbiota homeostasis. However, native banana starch was shown to alleviate intestinal barrier damage and mitigate colitis by increasing the relative abundances of Akkermansia and Oscillospira . Our findings demonstrate that individuals with colitis or bowel dysfunctions should exercise caution when consuming food rich in resistant starch to minimize potential adverse health effects.

works.title: α-Tocopherol-dependent occurrence of linoleic acid 11-hydroperoxide in triacylglycerol: what it signifies in food oxidation and quality
works.abstract: Although α-tocopherol (α-Toc) suppresses lipid oxidation overall, during linoleic acid oxidation it can paradoxically facilitate the formation of a unique hydroperoxide isomer bearing a hydroperoxyl group at the C11-position. Whether this isomer occurs in real foods and what it signifies in food oxidation and quality have remained unknown. Here, we initially applied a newly developed isomer-selective liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry method to intact triacylglycerol autoxidized in the presence of α-Toc and identified the isomer within the triacylglycerol molecule. Interestingly, its formation coincided with the emergence of the pro-oxidant properties of excess α-Toc, pointing to its potential as an indicator of pro-oxidative conditions. The isomer was scarcely detected in commercial oils, whereas the external addition of excess α-Toc enhanced its formation, suggesting that such pro-oxidative conditions were not prevalent in the examined oils. As an additional perspective on its decomposition, gas chromatography–mass spectrometry analysis revealed a range of volatiles, with heptanal and heptanoic acid as key compounds whose generation has long remained uncharacterized in linoleic acid oxidation. Together, these findings position the isomer as both a candidate marker of pro-oxidative conditions in foods and a possible contributor to food flavor, suggesting its significance for guiding food quality improvement.

works.title: Edible Biopolymer Coatings for Postharvest Preservation in Warm‐Chain Horticultural Supply Chain: Mechanisms, Materials, Design Strategies, and Future Directions
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.abstract: Fresh fruit and vegetable postharvest losses reach 30%-50% between harvest and consumption, concentrated in low- and middle-income countries where warm-chain supply chains (20°C-35°C, 55%-85% relative humidity, intermittent handling) replace the refrigerated cold chains conventional technology assumes. Edible coatings from polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids offer a non-refrigeration postharvest intervention, with efficacy confirmed under controlled laboratory conditions, but commercial adoption remains marginal. This review argues that the gap between laboratory performance and field outcomes is primarily a systems-design failure, in which existing formulations optimized for stable, refrigerated conditions are not engineered to maintain function under warm-chain variability. Biopolymer materials face a three-axis trade-off, unable to simultaneously satisfy moisture barrier performance, gas exchange selectivity, and thermal-hygroscopic stability, and all three degrade predictably under warm-chain conditions through mechanisms current formulation design does not account for. Bioactive release kinetics compound this failure by depleting protection before supply chain completion, while the absence of a commodity classification framework makes the research literature noncumulative. This review makes three contributions. It provides, to the authors' knowledge, among the first integrated analyses of biopolymer coating performance failure under warm-chain conditions, distinguished by its deployment-focused approach rather than a materials-cataloging one. It formalizes this into a three-axis framework showing that composite design is physically necessary for warm-chain applications, and proposes a four-pillar warm-chain design framework comprising predictive formulation modeling, controlled-release calibration, commodity-specific coating architecture, and standardized warm-chain validation protocols. A six-phase implementation pipeline and a commodity-specific application matrix operationalize this framework into a demonstrable pathway from formulation to field deployment.

De novo design of protein binders targeting the human sweet taste receptor as potential sweet proteins
works.abstract: There is growing interest in alternative sweeteners that reduce dietary sugar intake while maintaining desirable sensory properties. Natural sweet proteins offer high sweetness potency but are limited by natural diversity and challenges in production, stability, and formulation. In this study, we developed an integrated computational framework for de novo design and prioritization of protein binders targeting the extracellular domain (ECD) of the human sweet taste receptor subunit TAS1R2. The workflow combines RFdiffusion-based backbone generation, ProteinMPNN sequence design, Boltz-1 structural evaluation, static GBSA energetic assessment, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Designed binders targeted structurally relevant regions of the TAS1R2 Venus flytrap and cysteine-rich domains. Binder2 showed the strongest Boltz-1 structural confidence, whereas Binder1 exhibited the most favorable static GBSA estimate. Subsequent 200-ns MD simulations revealed distinct interaction profiles: Binder1 formed the largest and most interaction-rich interface, Binder2 maintained a persistent mixed polar/nonpolar network, and Binder3 showed greater conformational rearrangement and a more restricted interface. Advantame-bound TAS1R2 served as a structurally defined reference for trajectory-based analyses. These results demonstrate that receptor-guided de novo design can generate structurally diverse TAS1R2-binding proteins and support candidate prioritization for future experimental validation of receptor activation and sensory sweetness.

A glycoprotein from Hericium erinaceus attenuates metabolic disorders in type 2 diabetic mice
works.abstract: Hericium erinaceus is a well‑known edible and medicinal mushroom, yet its glycoproteins remain largely unexplored. In this study, a glycoprotein (HEP) was isolated from H. erinaceus and characterized by SDS–PAGE, PAS staining, FT–IR, and LC–MS/MS. Structural analysis revealed that HEP exhibits an α‑helix‑rich conformation with random coils and characteristic. The hypoglycemic effects of HEP were evaluated in a high‑fat diet combined with streptozotocin‑induced type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) mouse model. Twenty‑five male ICR mice were randomly divided into control, T2DM model, metformin positive control, and HEP low‑dose and high‑dose groups. After five weeks of dietary intervention and 1 week of streptozocin injection, HEP was administered orally for two consecutive weeks. HEP treatment significantly reduced fasting blood glucose, improved insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance, and alleviated dyslipidemia and hepatic steatosis. HEP was associated with reactivation of the hepatic PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, reduction of oxidative stress, and downregulation of pro‑inflammatory cytokines. Additionally, HEP reshaped the gut microbiota composition and reversed T2DM‑associated metabolic disturbances, with key metabolites correlated with diabetic parameters. This study highlights the potential of H. erinaceus as a natural nutraceutical candidates for managing T2DM.

Taxonomic and functional insights into brewery biofilms under amine-based lubricant exposure
works.abstract: Amine-based lubricants are widely used in breweries to reduce friction on conveyor systems and are often considered bacteriostatic, yet their impact on microbial biofilms remains largely unexplored. Here, we combined 16S/18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing with nanopore-based metagenomics to investigate biofilms from spray nozzles and conveyor belts in three breweries. Spray-associated biofilms were dominated by a conserved core of Gram-negative bacteria and enriched in genes involved in amine metabolism and oxidative stress responses, indicating functional adaptation to lubricant exposure. In contrast, biofilms collected near bottling units were dominated by lactic acid bacteria and yeasts and showed metabolic signatures consistent with beer-derived substrates. Notably, antibiotic resistance genes were positively correlated with stress-related genes, particularly in spray nozzle biofilms, suggesting co-occurrence under lubricant-associated stress. Together, these findings highlight the role of industrial lubricants as key ecological drivers shaping microbial community structure and resistance profiles in brewery environments.

works.title: Toxigenic potential of Aspergillus section Flavi and Fusarium spp. and mycotoxin accumulation in maize across two contrasting growing seasons
works.abstract: Maize is frequently contaminated by toxigenic fungi, mainly Fusarium spp. and Aspergillus section Flavi, which produce several mycotoxins and represent a major food safety concern. Climate change is expected to alter fungal communities in agroecosystems, potentially modifying mycotoxin contamination patterns in maize. This study compared mycotoxin accumulation and the mycotoxigenic potential of fungal isolates between two consecutive growing seasons characterized by contrasting climatic conditions (2023, hot/dry, and 2024, mild/wet) in maize samples from northeastern Spain. From 2023 and 2024, 853 Fusarium and 210 Aspergillus section Flavi isolates were obtained, and their toxigenic potential for fumonisins (FBs), deoxynivalenol (DON), zearalenone (ZEN), T-2/HT-2 toxins and aflatoxins (AFs) was assessed by HPLC, while natural mycotoxin contamination in the maize samples was determined by ELISA. The 2024 season was associated with a higher proportion of mycotoxin-producing Fusarium isolates and higher DON and ZEN concentrations in maize. DON and ZEN concentrations were positively correlated in both growing seasons, and the relative proportion of F. graminearum was positively associated with DON. F. proliferatum showed high FBs-producing potential in both seasons and a higher proportion of FBs-producing isolates than F. verticillioides. Although AFs-producing isolates were more frequent in 2023, AFs remained below the analytical LOD in all maize samples from both seasons. A. parasiticus showed high AF-producing capacity in vitro despite its relatively low occurrence. No significant correlations were detected between the in vitro toxigenic potential of fungal isolates and mycotoxin concentrations in the corresponding maize samples. Overall, contrasting seasonal conditions were associated with differences in toxigenic fungal profiles and mycotoxin accumulation in maize.

works.title: Engineering the UiO-66 Surface Microenvironment for Robust β-Glucosidase and Selective Production of Ginsenoside Rd
Preventive mechanisms of Potentilla longifolia against MASLD based on chemical profiling, network pharmacology, and metabolomics
works.abstract: Potentilla longifolia D. F. K. Schltdl. (GYC), a common edible vegetable in Inner Mongolia and a botanical resource historically recognized in northeastern China for its health-promoting benefits, was investigated for its prophylactic effects against metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). In this study, 25 major bioactive constituents were characterized via UHPLC-QE-MS, providing a chemical blueprint for subsequent integrated network pharmacology and untargeted metabolomics analysis. Metabolic profiling of serum and liver tissue identified 18 and 15 differential metabolites, respectively, highlighting the AMPK and NF-κB axes as primary regulatory hubs. In vivo and in vitro experimental validations demonstrated that GYC intervention effectively prevented high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity, hepatic steatosis, and early hepatic injury. Mechanistically, GYC maintained lipid homeostasis and early hepatic inflammatory responses by activating the AMPK signaling axis and suppressing the NF-κB/MAPK pathways. These findings provide a robust scientific rationale for utilizing GYC as a functional food resource or a promising prophylactic agent for the prevention of MASLD.
